false_positives.candidate:
No tests for the new retry/delete behaviour

The PR adds retry counting and a new deletion rule: a failed `scheduleSMS` increments retryCount, and rows with retryCount > 1 are deleted on the next run. None of this is covered by a test, including the off-by-one threshold (`gt: 1` means deletion after the second failure). A regression in the counting or the OR delete filter would go unnoticed.

Reminders with no sendTo or empty message never increment retryCount

retryCount is only incremented when `scheduleSMS` returns a falsy value or throws. If `sendTo` is missing (e.g. no `smsReminderNumber` on the booking) or the message is empty, the `if (message?.length && ... && sendTo)` check fails and nothing happens. The same applies to the earlier `continue` for a missing workflowStep or booking. Those reminders are never counted as failures, so the cron keeps re-processing them every run until `scheduledDate` passes. That is the exact behaviour the PR sets out to remove. A missing phone number is a common case of the 'invalid phone number' scenario in the description.

Unguarded prisma.update inside catch can abort the whole cron run

The catch block now runs `prisma.workflowReminder.update(...)` without its own try/catch. If that update throws (DB error, or the row was deleted concurrently so Prisma raises P2025), the exception escapes the `for` loop. The handler rejects, the endpoint returns a 500, and every remaining reminder in `unscheduledReminders` is skipped for that run. Previously one bad reminder only logged an error. Wrap the update in its own try/catch, or use `updateMany`, so a bookkeeping failure cannot stop the batch.

Unindexed retryCount in an OR condition on a large table

The delete's WHERE is now `(method AND scheduledDate) OR retryCount > 1`. The existing indexes (`[method, scheduled, scheduledDate]`, etc.) cannot serve the `retryCount` branch, so Postgres will likely fall back to a sequential scan of WorkflowReminder on every cron run. Scoping the second branch to `method = SMS` and `scheduled = false` would let the existing index apply.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getBaseConditions(), the else if (filterConditions) and final else branches are unreachable. This is because getAuthorizationConditions() always returns a non-null Prisma.Sql object, making authConditions always truthy, which means only the first two if/else if conditions are ever evaluated.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBaseConditions can return an unparenthesized OR expression that breaks authorization when callers append AND clauses

The org and team authorization conditions are built as `(A) OR (B)` with no outer parentheses. The eventTypeId filter has the same shape: `("eventTypeId" = X) OR ("eventParentId" = X)`. `getBaseConditions` only wraps them when both auth and filter conditions exist. In the `else if (authConditions) return authConditions;` path, which is the live path when no filters are set, it returns the bare `A OR B`. A caller writing `WHERE ${baseConditions} AND "createdAt" > ...` gets `A OR B AND C`, which SQL parses as `A OR (B AND C)`. The first branch of the authorization check then matches rows regardless of the extra filter. For an authorization predicate this is easy to get wrong silently. Wrap every returned fragment in parentheses, for example `Prisma.sql\`(${authConditions})\``, or parenthesize inside the `reduce` and in each builder. The final `else if (filterConditions)` and `NOTHING_CONDITION` branches are unreachable, because `authConditions` is always a truthy `Sql` object.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Fetching userIdsFromOrg only when teamsFromOrg.length > 0 can exclude org-level members for orgs without child teams; consider deriving from teamIds (which includes orgId) or removing the guard so org-only orgs still include member user bookings.

false_positives.candidate:
Caching tests removed and new service branches left uncovered

The "Caching" describe block was deleted, but `cachedAuthConditions` and `cachedFilterConditions` still exist in the service. Nothing now verifies that the second call reuses the cached value. The new `userIdsFromTeam.length > 0` and `userIdsFromOrg.length > 0` branches are also never exercised with an empty list. The team test always has a member, and there is no case for a team that is not a child of the org (`NOTHING_CONDITION`) or a team with no members. Restore the caching tests with the new `Prisma.sql` expectations and add cases for the empty-member and non-child-team branches.

Only the user-scope path is tested end to end against the database

`getBaseConditions` is executed with `$queryRaw` only for `scope: "user"` plus an eventType filter. The org/team scopes with `OR` combinations, `= ANY($n)` array parameters, and the combined auth-plus-filter case are only compared as SQL objects and never run against Postgres. The exact-equality tests would pass even if the SQL were invalid or had wrong precedence, for example the bare-OR problem when combined with other clauses. Add at least one execution test for org or team scope with a filter.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unrelated, macOS-only helper script added; breaks on Linux and exits 0 on failure

The script is not wired into anything and is unrelated to this feature. `sed -i '' -E ...` is BSD/macOS syntax; with GNU sed the empty string is parsed as the script and the real expression as a filename, so the .env update fails on Linux. `ENV_FILE="../.env"` depends on the caller's cwd. `cleanup` always does `exit 0`, so the rate-limit and failed-URL paths report success. It also silently rewrites `.env`. Remove it from this PR or make it portable and correct.

true_positives.golden_comment: Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Authorization failure throws a plain Error instead of TRPCError

When the credential is missing or belongs to another user, the handler throws `new Error(...)`. tRPC maps this to a generic 500 INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR and it gets logged as a server error. Use `TRPCError` with `NOT_FOUND` or `FORBIDDEN`, as other handlers do. Negative in-memory delegation credential IDs also fall into this branch and will surface as 500s. The input schema in `_router.tsx` is also an inline `z.number()`, with no `.int()` and no separate schema file like the sibling procedures.

true_positives.golden_comment: Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache timestamp formatted with hard-coded en-US locale

`new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", ...)` ignores the user's locale and the app's i18n setting. Non-English users see US-style dates (M/D/YY) inside an otherwise translated string. Use the user's locale (for example `i18n.language`) or the existing date-formatting helpers.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.

false_positives.candidate:
Backfill with NOW() makes all legacy cache rows report the migration time as last updated; header comment is wrong

Every pre-existing `CalendarCache` row gets `updatedAt = <migration time>`. The new UI will then show "Last updated" as the deploy time for entries that may be weeks old, which is misleading. Backfilling from an existing signal such as `expiresAt - 30 days` would be more accurate. The warning at the top of the file (lines 1-6) says the column was added "without a default value" and "is not possible if the table is not empty". That contradicts the statement below it, which adds a default. It is leftover auto-generated text and should be removed.

Deleting cache does not refresh connectedCalendars, so the UI keeps showing stale cache status

`deleteCacheMutation` only shows a toast and calls `onSuccess?.()`. It never invalidates `utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars`. The `disconnectMutation` in the same file does invalidate it in `onSettled`. `onSuccess` is the optional `onChanged` prop, and the wrapper passes whatever the parent gave it, which may be undefined. After a successful delete, `cacheUpdatedAt` stays cached, so the dropdown still shows the old "Last updated" timestamp and still offers "Delete cached data". The test plan expects "UI updates appropriately", which this does not do. Invalidate the query in the delete mutation.

Empty fixed-width wrapper rendered when dropdown has nothing to show

The old code only rendered the `<div className="flex w-32 justify-end">` when the credential could be disconnected. Now the wrapper is always rendered, but `CredentialActionsDropdown` returns `null` for delegation or read-only credentials with no cache. This leaves an empty 8rem-wide block in the card header and in the Alert's actions area. The same applies to the second usage at line 123. Render the wrapper only when the dropdown has content, or move it inside the component.

Extra unconditional updateMany on every cache refresh with empty data

`SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})` now runs after every `fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache`, which is called from the webhook path. It relies on Prisma implicitly bumping `@updatedAt` for an empty update, and it rewrites every SelectedCalendar row of the credential, including event-type-level rows. It runs even when no calendars were processed. The PR notes admit the UI does not use `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt` (it uses `CalendarCache.updatedAt`), so this is a pure extra write on a hot path. Drop it, or restrict it to a real requirement.

No tests for new repository method, tRPC handler, or dropdown component

The PR adds `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` (a groupBy with `_max`), a new `deleteCache` mutation with an ownership check, the `cacheUpdatedAt` enrichment in `connectedCalendarsHandler`, and a component with conditional rendering. None of these has a unit or integration test. The ownership check in `deleteCacheHandler` and the empty-result and negative-credential-ID cases in the enrichment are the most important to cover.

Unrelated change: dev:cron now relies on undeclared tsx via npx

Switching `dev:cron` from `ts-node` to `npx tsx` is unrelated to calendar cache. `tsx` is not declared in any dependency list, so `npx` downloads it at run time, unpinned and unreproducible. Other scripts in this file still use `ts-node`. Either keep `ts-node` or add `tsx` as a devDependency, and ideally put the change in a separate PR.

true_positives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
immediateDelete branch swallows SendGrid errors and never records the cancellation

In the `immediateDelete` branch the function POSTs the cancel to SendGrid and returns. It neither deletes the reminder row nor sets `cancelled`. If the request fails (for example at the 100 pending-cancellation limit), the outer catch only logs, so there is no fallback and the cron cannot retry. If the request succeeds, the row lingers until the scheduled date passes. This only works for callers whose rows are cascade-deleted afterwards (workflow or step deletion). For callers whose rows persist, such as the reschedule path, a failed cancel is lost. The branch should fall back to flagging `cancelled` on failure, or callers whose rows persist should not use it.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.

The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.

false_positives.candidate:
No tests for the new deferred-cancellation flow

The fix changes the contract of `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` and `deleteScheduledSMSReminder` and adds a new cron phase. It also rewires cancel, reschedule, workflow-update and workflow-delete paths. No tests were added for any of it: setting `cancelled`, the one-hour cancellation window, deleting rows after a successful cancel, or behaviour when SendGrid fails. The earlier fix in #6991 had to be redone because it was never exercised against SendGrid's real limits, so regression coverage matters here.

One failing SendGrid cancel aborts the whole batch and blocks later cancellations on every run

The cancel loop sits in a single try/catch. The `prisma.workflowReminder.delete(...)` calls are lazy PrismaPromises that only run at `await Promise.all(...)` after the loop. If any `client.request` throws (invalid or expired batch_id, rate limit, transient error), the loop exits and none of the deletes run, including those for reminders already cancelled. Reminders after the failing one are never processed. The failing row is still `cancelled: true` with a date inside the next hour, so it is retried first on every 15-minute run and fails again. All later cancelled reminders then go out as emails. Each reminder should be handled in its own try/catch, and its row deleted right after its own successful cancel.

Shared @sendgrid/client is never given the API key in this module, so the new cancel calls may be unauthenticated

This file only calls `sgMail.setApiKey(...)`. `@sendgrid/mail` uses its own internal Client instance, so that does not configure the default `@sendgrid/client` singleton used for `client.request`. Nothing in this module calls `client.setApiKey`. The new cancellation loop depends entirely on `client.request`. If the singleton has no key in the cron's process, every cancel returns 401. That error is swallowed by the try/catch (`console.log`), so nothing is cancelled and the emails still go out, silently. Add `client.setApiKey(sendgridAPIKey)` here, as emailReminderManager does.

Unused `Prisma` import and type imports turned into value imports

After the `PrismaPromise<Prisma.BatchPayload>[]` code was removed, `Prisma` is no longer used in this file, so it is an unused import (a lint failure). `PrismaPromise` was also changed from `import type` to a regular value import even though it is only used as a type. The same pattern appears in handleNewBooking.ts, where `App`, `Credential`, `EventTypeCustomInput` and `Prisma` were moved from `import type` to a value import. Restore the type-only imports and drop `Prisma`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
async forEach callback inside try/catch: errors are no longer caught and deletions are not awaited

The callback was made `async` so it can `await getCalendar(...)`. `forEach` ignores the returned promise, so the surrounding `try/catch` can no longer catch a `getCalendar` failure or a `deleteEvent`/`deleteMeeting` rejection. Previously a synchronous throw from `getCalendar` was caught and logged. Now the error becomes an unhandled promise rejection. The function also continues to send emails and returns `true` before the calendar and video deletions finish. In serverless environments the work can be cut off. Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...))` inside the try block.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully

false_positives.candidate:
Recurring-cancel path pushes into apiDeletes from an unawaited async forEach, after Promise.all has already run

In the `allRemainingBookings` branch, `.forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(credential); ... apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent) })` is not awaited. It also pushes the resolved result rather than the promise. `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` runs later and sees an `apiDeletes` array that these callbacks have not populated yet. The calendar deletions for recurring bookings are therefore never awaited, and their failures are unhandled rejections. Adding `await getCalendar` inside the callback delays the first `deleteEvent` call further, so a response (or serverless freeze) can happen before any deletion starts. Replace with a `for...of` loop or `Promise.all(map(...))` and push the promises.

async forEach callback inside try/catch: errors are no longer caught and deletions are not awaited

Same issue as the vital reschedule. `forEach(async ...)` discards the promises, so the `try/catch` around it is now dead for any rejection from `getCalendar`, `deleteEvent` or `deleteMeeting`; these become unhandled rejections. The reschedule flow does not wait for the external deletions before sending emails and returning. Replace with `await Promise.all(refs.map(async ...))` so errors are logged and the work completes.

import() calls in the object literal run eagerly, so every app still loads at module evaluation

Each entry is `import("./x")` evaluated directly in the object literal. All ~29 dynamic imports start the moment `@calcom/app-store` is first imported, so every app package is still loaded on first use of the store. This gives no lazy loading, and the module graph still pulls in every app. It also adds overhead: the promises are created up front, and call sites must now `await` them. An app whose import fails produces an unhandled rejection at startup. It then rejects on every later lookup instead of being skipped. To get lazy behaviour, store thunks (`() => import("./x")`) and invoke only the one needed.

requestReschedule: async forEach leaves calendar/video deletions unawaited and rejections unhandled

Making the `forEach` callback async to `await getCalendar` means the mutation neither awaits nor handles failures of `getCalendar`, `deleteEvent` or `deleteMeeting`. There is no `try/catch` here at all. A failing integration produces an unhandled rejection, which can crash the Node process or be silently dropped. The mutation also returns, after sending emails and webhooks, before the external events are actually removed. Collect the promises and `await Promise.all(...)`, with error handling.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Working-hours check is wrong: `end` equals `start`, and multiple ranges per day reject everything

`const end = slotStartTime.hour()*60 + slotStartTime.minute()` is identical to `start`. It should be based on the slot end time, so a slot that runs past the end of working hours is never caught. The `find` also returns true (slot unavailable) whenever any working-hours entry for that weekday does not contain the slot. Users with split schedules (e.g. 09-12 and 13-17) produce two entries for the same day, and any slot is outside at least one of them, so nearly all slots are rejected. Because this check is now applied to every fixed and loose host, it is a regression for those schedules. It should reject only when no entry contains the slot. Working hours are also compared against the UTC weekday and minutes of the slot, which needs care for schedules that cross UTC midnight.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dayjs objects compared with === (always false)

`dayjs(date.start).add(...) === dayjs(date.end).add(...)` compares two distinct object references, so it is never true. The intended "zero-length override means unavailable" branch is dead code. Use `.isSame()` or compare the underlying values.

false_positives.candidate:
Fixed-host round-robin date-override fix has no test; new timezone test is weak

The headline fix is that fixed hosts' date overrides must be respected in round-robin events, but no test covers it: no scenario with a fixed host that has an override and a round-robin host that does not. None covers multiple override ranges on one day, slots overlapping an override boundary, or overrides crossing midnight or UTC midnight, which are exactly where the new logic is fragile. The added timezone test (Dhaka) only shifts by 30 minutes and expects identical UTC slots. The `toHaveTimeSlots` matcher also passes when the actual list is shorter than the expected list, so missing slots would go unnoticed.

Multiple date-override ranges on the same day make most slots unavailable

`dateOverrides.find(...)` returns true (slot rejected) as soon as ANY override range on that day does not contain the slot. A host with two override intervals on one date (e.g. 09:00-11:00 and 14:00-16:00) is a supported setup. A slot at 14:30 is outside the first interval, so `find` returns true on it and the slot is rejected even though it is inside the second. The check needs to pass when the slot fits in at least one same-day override, and fail only when it fits in none. As written, the new logic wrongly drops valid slots for fixed hosts, and for collective and loose hosts too, since all of them now go through this check.

Override-to-slot matching uses the UTC calendar day and breaks for overrides crossing UTC midnight

An override is matched to a slot only when the UTC date of the shifted `override.start` equals the UTC date of `slotStartTime`. For organizers far from UTC, an override that begins on one UTC day and ends on the next (e.g. 10:00-18:00 PST is 18:00-02:00 UTC) will not match slots falling on the second UTC day. Those slots are then treated as having no override and fall through to the normal working-hours/busy logic. This can wrongly allow or deny them, which defeats the override.

Parsing `override.start.toString()` is lossy and environment-dependent

`dayjs(override.start.toString())` goes through `Date.prototype.toString()`, which yields a locale/host-timezone formatted string without milliseconds that is re-parsed by the engine. Pass `override.start` directly. Also `override.timeZone` is optional in `TimeRange`, and `.tz(undefined)` silently falls back to the default zone instead of failing visibly.

Slots that only partially overlap a date override are treated as available

The override test only rejects a slot if `slotEnd <= override.start` or `slotStart > override.end`. A slot that starts before the override and ends inside it is accepted. A slot that starts inside the override and ends after `override.end` is accepted. A slot starting exactly at `override.end` is accepted, because `isAfter` is strict. Example: with a fixed-host override of 10:00-11:00, a 10:30-11:30 or 11:00-12:00 slot generated from another host's availability passes. This is the situation the PR is meant to prevent (RR events booked when the fixed host is unavailable). The condition should be that the whole slot lies in `[override.start, override.end]`, i.e. reject when `slotStart < start` or `slotEnd > end`.

Timezone-shifted overrides can wrap past midnight and land on the wrong invitee day

The override is selected for an invitee day by `activeOverrides` using the unshifted (organizer-wall-clock-as-UTC) `override.start`. Only afterwards is the invitee-organizer offset added and reduced to `hour()*60+minute()`. Two problems follow. (1) If the shift pushes the start/end past midnight, the minutes wrap modulo 24h, so start or end becomes a small number and the range is either dropped (`start >= end` is skipped in `buildSlots`) or shown on the wrong day. (2) The day the override is attached to is computed before the shift. With a large timezone gap (e.g. organizer in Kolkata with a 20:00-23:00 override, invitee in Tokyo) the override can be attached to the day after the one it really falls on. The shifted instant, not the raw one, should be used for both the day filter and the minute-of-day computation.

true_positives.golden_comment: OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OAuth `state` is a static, guessable value, so it gives no CSRF protection

`state` is `pipeline.signature`, which the tests pin to the constant `9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3`. That is a deterministic hash of the pipeline view classes, not a per-flow random nonce. Every user and session therefore gets the same value, and an attacker can craft `/extensions/github/setup/?code=...&state=<known>` links that pass the check. An OAuth `state` must be unpredictable and tied to the user's session. Also, `!=` is a non-constant-time comparison; use `constant_time_compare`. As written, the PR's claim that a mismatching `state` is rejected adds little real protection.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
KeyError when the existing Integration has no `sender` metadata

`integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` assumes every pre-existing Integration carries webhook-provided `sender` metadata. `build_integration` only sets `sender` from `state.get("sender")`, and nothing in this pipeline ever binds that key. The updated `test_basic_flow` also shows an Integration created through the pipeline with no `sender` in its metadata. If such an Integration remains without an OrganizationIntegration, for example after one org is uninstalled, a legacy record, or an install created through the pipeline, this lookup raises `KeyError`. The user gets a 500 instead of the friendly error page, and the install is blocked. Use `.get("sender", {}).get("login")` and treat a missing sender as a controlled failure, or define explicit behaviour for it.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Null reference if github_authenticated_user state is missing

false_positives.candidate:
Authenticated-user check is skipped whenever the Integration row doesn't exist yet

The new `github_authenticated_user` vs `sender.login` comparison only runs when an Integration with that `external_id` already exists. It is created by the `installation` webhook. When `Integration.DoesNotExist` is raised, the code calls `pipeline.next_step()` without checking that the OAuth-authenticated user is the one who installed the app. Anyone who learns an installation_id can therefore finish the pipeline before the webhook has been processed, or if it was delayed or lost, and bind someone else's installation to their org. The check depends on a webhook race. A robust fix would verify against GitHub directly, for example by confirming the installation appears in `GET /user/installations` for the user token. The OAuth user token is already available at that point but is discarded after reading `login`.

Network and HTTP errors in the token exchange and user lookup are not handled

Only `safe_urlread` and decoding are inside the `try`. `safe_urlopen(...)` on line 423 can raise connection, timeout or SSL errors, and `get_user_info(...)` on line 434 calls `raise_for_status()`, so an invalid or expired token raises `HTTPError`. Either failure surfaces as an unhandled 500 in the middle of the install dialog, not the 'Invalid installation request' page the PR describes for these cases. The existing `OAuth2CallbackView.exchange_token`, which this code is modelled on, wraps the whole exchange in exception handling. The failure paths also log nothing, so a failed exchange gives support and debugging no signal.

New failure and success paths of the validation are untested

Only the user-mismatch case is covered, and only incidentally the state mismatch. There are no tests for: a failed token exchange (no `access_token` in the response); a `/user` response without `login`; or the positive case where an Integration with webhook-provided `sender` already exists, has no OrganizationIntegration, and the authenticated user matches. That last case is the main new success path of `GitHubInstallation`. There is also no test for an existing Integration lacking `sender` metadata, which would currently raise `KeyError`. `assert_setup_flow` additionally hard-codes `responses.calls[2]`, which silently breaks whenever the number of HTTP calls in the flow changes.

`test_installation_not_found` no longer exercises the installation-not-found path

The test now sends `state=ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05`, which differs from the pipeline signature `9cae5e...`. The request is therefore rejected by the `state` mismatch check in `OAuthLoginView` before the 404 from `/app/installations/...` is ever reached. It asserts the generic 'Invalid installation request.' text. So it now covers state mismatch under a misleading name, and the `The GitHub installation could not be found.` branch in `build_integration` has lost its coverage. Use the valid state for this test, and add a separate test for state mismatch.

true_positives.golden_comment: The AssignmentSource dataclass uses queued: datetime = timezone.now() as a default field value, which evaluates timezone.now() once at class definition time and shares that single datetime instance across all objects.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`queued` default is evaluated once at import time, not per instance

`queued: datetime = timezone.now()` calls `timezone.now()` once, when the class body executes at module import. Every `AssignmentSource` created without an explicit `queued` therefore gets the same process-start timestamp, not the time the assignment was queued. The field exists to record when the source was queued, so any later use for ordering, staleness checks or logging will see wrong data. The fix is `field(default_factory=timezone.now)`. `test_to_dict` only asserts `queued is not None`, so it passes despite this bug.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The method name has a typo: test_from_dict_inalid_data should be test_from_dict_invalid_data.
Method name says 'empty_array' but tests empty dict - consider renaming to 'test_from_dict_empty_dict' for clarity.
to_dict() returns a datetime for queued; if this dict is passed in task kwargs (e.g., via apply_async), JSON serialization may fail depending on the serializer, which can cause enqueue errors.

false_positives.candidate:
Cycle-breaking is not tested on the deassign path or end-to-end through inbound sync

The only new test of the suppression behaviour covers `GroupAssignee.objects.assign` with an `AssignmentSource` that matches the integration. Three paths are untested. First, `deassign(..., assignment_source=...)` never has its suppression asserted. Second, `sync_group_assignee_inbound` (the actual webhook entry point that builds the source, for both assign and deassign) is never checked for skipping the outbound call. The existing inbound tests don't assert that `sync_assignee_outbound` is not called. Third, there is no test that a different integration's source still propagates outward, which the `should_sync` comment says is intended. true_positives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) is False for spawn processes, so hung flushers are never killed

The processes are created with `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process`, which is `SpawnProcess`. `SpawnProcess` subclasses `BaseProcess` directly and is not a subclass of `multiprocessing.Process` (that is `context.Process`). The new `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` guard around `process.kill()` is therefore always False in production, and the kill never runs. The old code called `self.process.kill()` unconditionally. When the cause is `hang`, the stuck process is now left running and `_create_process_for_shards` starts a second flusher for the same shards. Two flushers then consume and produce the same segments concurrently, and every further restart leaks one more process. Use `hasattr(process, 'kill')` or check `multiprocessing.context.BaseProcess`/`SpawnProcess` instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.

The test starts with `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)`, which replaces `time.sleep` globally. The new `time.sleep(0.1)`, commented "Give flusher threads time to process after drift change", therefore does nothing. `step.join()` sets `stopped` immediately, and the flusher thread can exit its `while not stopped.value` loop before it flushes. Wait on a condition (poll until `messages` is non-empty, with a timeout) or use the real sleep (`monkeypatch.undo()` or a saved reference) for this wait.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join() never terminates spawned processes, and its deadline break skips cleanup for the rest

Two problems in `join()`. First, `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` is False for `SpawnProcess`, so `process.terminate()` never runs for real flusher processes. Second, the new `if remaining_time <= 0: break` leaves the loop before reaching terminate for the current and all remaining processes. If the deadline expires while waiting on an early process, the later processes are neither waited on nor terminated. Terminate should run for every process regardless of the deadline, and the type check needs to match `SpawnProcess`.

false_positives.candidate:
Memory info is polled once per per-process buffer on every submit

`submit()` now loops over every per-process `SpansBuffer` and extends `memory_infos` with `buffer.get_memory_info()` for each one. That method appears to report on the whole Redis cluster rather than just the buffer's shards. If so, each submit issues N times the INFO calls, and `used` and `available` are both inflated by N. The ratio stays the same, so the result is correct but wasteful. The same applies to `record_stored_segments` per buffer. Query memory once, from a single buffer.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Error-handling test asserts no offsets are committed, contradicting its docstring and the actual behavior

The docstring says "errors in processing don't block offset commits for other messages". The assertion `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets` checks that nothing was committed. In the implementation, a failing item still has its offset completed in the `finally`, so both offsets 100 and 101 become committable and are committed on the next 1s commit tick. The test only passes because it stops waiting about 0.2s after processing, before the commit loop fires. It is timing-dependent and verifies nothing about the intended behavior. It should wait for the commit and assert that offset 102 is committed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.

false_positives.candidate:
Commit logic assumes strictly contiguous Kafka offsets and stalls permanently on any gap

`get_committable_offsets` walks `range(start, max_offset + 1)` and stops at the first offset that is not in `all_offsets`. Kafka partitions can legitimately have non-consecutive offsets (compaction, transaction control records, messages skipped or filtered upstream). After `mark_committed` trims the set, a single missing offset means `highest_committable` never advances past it. The consumer then stops committing for that partition forever, `all_offsets` grows without bound, and a restart replays everything since the gap. `test_offset_gaps_block_commits` encodes this behavior as desired. A safer approach is to track only the offsets actually submitted, in order, and commit up to the smallest outstanding offset.

Distribution test is flaky because str hash is randomized per process, and the ordering/concurrency tests do not check ordering or concurrency

`test_different_groups_distributed` asserts that 20 string group keys cover all 3 queues. `hash(str)` is salted per interpreter run, so there is roughly a 0.1% chance on any run that some queue is never hit, which makes the test flaky. Separately, `test_preserves_order_within_group` and `test_concurrent_processing_different_groups` in the strategy tests only check that the result count equals the number submitted, even though their names and docstrings claim ordering and concurrency are verified. `test_concurrent_processing_across_groups` has the same problem, since it never checks that groups actually run in parallel.

Offsets are committed from a background thread, but arroyo's commit callback and KafkaConsumer are not thread-safe

`_commit_loop` runs on its own daemon thread and calls `self.commit_function(...)`, which wraps arroyo's `commit` callback. That callback stages and commits offsets on the `KafkaConsumer`, whose state is owned by the main `StreamProcessor` thread; arroyo does not support calling it concurrently with `poll`/`_run_once`. This can race with the main thread's own consumer calls. It can also commit offsets for partitions that have just been revoked, which makes `stage_offsets` raise. When that raise happens, `mark_committed` is skipped. The tracker never forgets the revoked partition, so the same failing commit is retried and logged every second indefinitely. Commits should be handed back to the main thread, for example by recording the committable offsets and calling `commit` from `poll()`.

Queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure despite the class docstring promising it

`queue.Queue()` is created without `maxsize`, and `submit()` never blocks or raises `MessageRejected`. The strategy's docstring claims "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but there is none. If any worker is slow (the exact scenario this PR targets) or the DB is degraded, the consumer keeps reading from Kafka at full speed. Queue depth, the `WorkItem`s (which hold the full Kafka message) and the offset tracker sets all grow without bound, which risks OOM. Meanwhile no offsets are committed because commits are contiguous. Use a bounded queue and translate a full queue into `MessageRejected` so arroyo applies backpressure, or at least fix the docstring.

Shutdown joins workers sequentially with 5s each, never flushes a final commit, and 'graceful' drain is not honored

`FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` joins each worker with a 5s timeout one after another. If several workers are busy, `terminate()` or `close()` can block for up to 5s × num_queues (100s with the default 20), which stalls rebalances and shutdown. `worker.shutdown = True` also makes workers exit after the current item, so `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` never actually drains the remaining queued items. Neither `close()` nor `terminate()` does a final commit of offsets that finished processing since the last 1s tick, so those messages are reprocessed on restart. `join(timeout)` also ignores its timeout argument.

Strategy close()/terminate() shuts down the factory-owned queue pool, so messages are silently dropped and committed after the first rebalance

The `FixedQueuePool` and its `OffsetTracker` are created once in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` and shared by every strategy from `create_with_partitions`. Arroyo calls `close()`/`join()` on the strategy at every rebalance, and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()`/`terminate()` call `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`. That permanently shuts down all queues and workers. The factory still holds the dead pool (`queue_pool` is only set to None in `factory.shutdown()`), so the next strategy gets the same pool. Every `work_queue.put()` then raises `queue.ShutDown`. `submit()` catches `Exception`, marks the offset as added and completed, and moves on. The result is that after the first rebalance every message is dropped without being processed, and its offset is still committed. The tracker also keeps `last_committed`, `all_offsets` and `outstanding` for partitions that were revoked or reassigned. The strategy should not own the shared pool's lifecycle. Either build the pool and tracker per strategy, or leave them running in `close()` and only stop them from `factory.shutdown()`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial-cache test passes even if the denial cache is ignored

The test comment says it allows access in `permCache` 'to prove this is not checked', but the cached map is `{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}`, which also denies. Without the denial-cache lookup, `Check` would see a cached deny, fall back to the default `fakeStore` (no permissions), and still return `Allowed=false`. The test therefore cannot tell whether the denial short-circuit works. It should seed an allowing permission (`true`, or a store that grants access) and assert the store is not called. There is also no test that a DB-confirmed deny populates `permDenialCache`, and none that a later identical check skips the DB.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key is ambiguous because fields are joined with '_' and names can contain '_'

The key is `ns.perm_<uid>_<action>_<name>_<parent>`, and Grafana dashboard and folder UIDs may contain underscores. `name="a_b", parent="c"` and `name="a", parent="b_c"` produce the same key, so a denial for one resource denies the other for the whole TTL. The key also shares the `.perm_<uid>_<action>` prefix with `userPermCacheKey`, so the two caches are only kept apart by their value types. Use a distinct prefix such as `perm_denial_` and a separator that cannot occur in the fields, or hash the parts.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache key omits identity type, so denials leak between anonymous and render subjects

`userPermDenialCacheKey` is built from namespace, `checkReq.UserUID`, action, name and parent. The identity type is not part of the key. `Check` reads the denial cache before it looks at `IdentityType`. `anonymous:0` and `render:0` both have UID `0`, so they share a key. The existing permission cache avoids this by using a separate `anonymousPermCacheKey`. If anonymous is denied `dashboards:read` on dash1, a later `render:0` check for the same dashboard hits that entry and is wrongly denied, even though the renderer is granted read on everything. The reverse also happens: a render denial for a write action can deny an anonymous Editor. Include the identity type in the key, or use a separate prefix per type.

Denials computed from a possibly stale folder tree are cached with no invalidation

After the DB re-query, `checkPermission` calls `checkInheritedPermissions`, which uses `buildFolderTree`. That tree is itself cached for 30s and is not refreshed by the permission re-query. For a newly created nested folder whose permission comes only from an ancestor, the stale tree does not contain the folder, so the check is denied. That result is then stored in the denial cache for another 30s, with no way to clear it when the folder tree or the user's permissions change. Access to newly created resources can stay denied for up to a minute even though the re-query was meant to fix exactly this case.

Every distinct denied resource now triggers a full DB permission re-query

In `Check`, when the cached scope map does not allow the request, the code always falls through to `getIdentityPermissions`. That runs `GetUserBasicRole`, `ListUserTeams` and `GetUserPermissions` against the DB, and `getUserPermissions` no longer short-circuits on the cache. The denial cache is keyed per (user, action, name, parent), so it only helps for repeats of the exact same resource. A user who is legitimately denied on many different dashboards or folders, for example a UI list of items or a scan, causes one DB permission query per distinct resource within each 30s window. Singleflight only merges concurrent calls. This removes most of the protection the permission cache gave and can amplify load on the DB. Consider rate-limiting the refresh per user/action, or negative-caching at the (user, action) level for a short time after a refresh.
