This is a breaking contract change that the PR description (a rename and move) does not mention.

FromContext silently drops contextual attributes if the assertion fails

If `d.l.FromContext(ctx)` returns anything other than `*log.ConcreteLogger`, the code falls back to `d.New()`. That logger has none of the request's contextual attributes (pluginId, endpoint, dsUID, traceID, etc.), and nothing signals that they were lost. The middleware would then emit 'Plugin Request Completed' without the fields that were previously always added explicitly. The wrapper holds a `*ConcreteLogger` and relies on a type assertion on an interface return, which is fragile. The fallback at least deserves a comment or a test.

No tests for the new ContextualLoggerMiddleware or the changed LoggerMiddleware

The contextual-logger logic moved out of the metrics middleware into this new middleware, and LoggerMiddleware dropped its manual pluginId/endpoint/dsName/dsUID/uname/traceID params in favour of `logger.FromContext(ctx)`. The only test change is a rename in the metrics test. Nothing verifies that `instrumentContext` attaches the expected attributes for each endpoint. Nothing verifies that the logger middleware still emits those fields, including the traceID it used to add explicitly, or that the middleware ordering works. A regression in the log fields of 'Plugin Request Completed' would go unnoticed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Check-then-insert on the device limit is racy and can exceed the configured limit

`CreateOrUpdateDevice` runs `CountDevices` in one session and then does the `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT` in a separate session, with no transaction or lock. N concurrent requests from N new devices can all read `count < deviceLimit` and all insert, so the table can overshoot the limit, and more so with several Grafana instances. Fix: do the count and insert atomically, for example `INSERT ... SELECT ... WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) ...) < limit`, or use a serialized transaction. At minimum, document the limit as approximate.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Local cache entry is set before the store call, so a rejected device bypasses the limit on its next request

`tagDeviceUI` calls `localCache.SetDefault(key, ...)` before `CreateOrUpdateDevice`. When the store returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, the cache key is already set. The first request from that device is rejected. Every later request within the cache TTL (29 minutes) hits `localCache.Get(key)`, returns nil and is authenticated as anonymous without being recorded. The limit is therefore only enforced once per device per TTL, so any over-limit device gets through on retry or page reload. The same ordering also means a transient DB error suppresses retries for 29 minutes. Fix: set the cache entry only after `CreateOrUpdateDevice` succeeds, or delete it on error.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
Device limit behavior is only minimally tested

Only one test covers the limit: a new device is rejected once the limit is reached. Nothing tests that an existing device within the 30-day window can still be updated at the limit, or that a device older than 30 days is rejected. Nothing covers the `Anonymous.Authenticate` change that now returns an error on `ErrDeviceLimitReached`. Nothing covers the local-cache interaction, which is where the real bug in this change sits. A test for repeated requests from a rejected device would have caught it.

Device tagging moved from a background goroutine into the authentication path

`TagDevice` used to run in a goroutine with its own 2-minute timeout and panic recovery. It now runs synchronously on the request context. Every anonymous request from an uncached device now waits for DB work: a `COUNT(*)` when a limit is set, plus a write. A slow or locked DB therefore slows or fails anonymous requests. Request cancellation also aborts the tagging write. The panic recovery that guarded this code is gone as well. Only the limit-reached error needs to be synchronous. Consider keeping the non-limit path async, or at least a bounded timeout.

New `device_limit` option is undocumented

The new `[auth.anonymous] device_limit` setting is read here, but it is not added to `conf/defaults.ini`, `conf/sample.ini` or the docs. The PR description is also an empty template. It is not documented that 0 (or any non-positive value) means unlimited, that the limit counts devices seen in the last 30 days, or that over-limit new devices are rejected with an authentication error. Operators cannot discover or safely use the setting.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Debug logging left in at Error level, dumping every ID list on each batch

Six `r.log.Error(...)` calls (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579) run unconditionally in the cleanup loop. They log the full `ids` slice, the SQL condition, and an `err` value that is always nil at that point. Each batch emits two Error-level lines, including the final empty batch when there is nothing to clean. With the batch size configurable, the ID list can reach tens of thousands of entries per line. Together with the 1-minute ticker, this floods the error logs and trips alerting on error-level logs even when nothing went wrong. These look like debugging leftovers. Remove them, or log only counts at Debug level.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup ticker interval changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute

The cleanup service ticker is changed from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1`. This is unrelated to the deadlock fix and is not mentioned in the PR description. It looks like a local-testing leftover. It makes every cleanup job (snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, short URLs, query history) run 10x more often. The annotation cleanup now runs a SELECT plus a DELETE per batch, so this raises load and contention on the annotation table, the very thing this PR is meant to reduce. It also multiplies the log noise from the Error-level logging. Revert to 10 minutes.

false_positives.candidate:
Bound-parameter IN list can exceed driver placeholder limits on Postgres/MySQL for large batch sizes

Outside SQLite, `deleteByIDs` builds `DELETE ... WHERE id IN (?,?,...)` with one placeholder per ID, so the number of placeholders equals `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize`. Postgres and MySQL prepared statements cap placeholders at 65535. The old query embedded the limit in SQL and used no parameters, so any batch size worked. With this change, a deployment that configures a batch size above that cap will fail every cleanup run with a driver error. The special case only handles SQLite (threshold 999). Chunk the IDs, or inline the integer IDs for all dialects (they are int64, so this is safe).

true_positives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete puts the un-annotated logger into the context instead of the enriched one

`ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` discards the per-call `log` (name, kind, method) that was just built. All other methods use `klog.NewContext(ctx, log)`. Logs emitted downstream from the context lose the request attributes. It should use `log`.

true_positives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Legacy DeleteCollection duration is recorded as a storage duration

Inside the goroutine that calls `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection`, the result is recorded with `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ..., startLegacy)`. It should be `recordLegacyDuration`. Legacy latency and errors are attributed to the storage metrics, which double-counts storage and hides legacy failures.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete success metric uses `name` instead of `options.Kind` as the label

Every other metric call passes `options.Kind` as the name/kind label. The success path of Delete passes `name` (the object name). This produces one label value per deleted object, which is a high-cardinality metric. It also splits the success series from the error series, which uses `options.Kind`. It should be `options.Kind`.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes derive their context from the request context, which is cancelled when the handler returns

Each goroutine (Create l.51, Delete l.110, Update l.135, DeleteCollection l.163) does `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` on the request-scoped `ctx`. The API server cancels that context as soon as the HTTP handler returns, and the goroutine intentionally outlives the handler. The legacy write will therefore usually run with an already-cancelled context and fail or abort. The legacy store silently drifts from unified storage, which is the opposite of the 'safe measure' described in the PR. Use `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (or a fresh background context carrying the logger) as the parent of the timeout context.

Legacy update re-applies the original objInfo instead of the object written to storage

The previous implementation wrapped the result in `updateWrapper` so legacy stored exactly the object that unified storage persisted. Now the goroutine calls `d.Legacy.Update(ctx, name, objInfo, ...)` with the raw `objInfo`. For patch/apply requests the update is re-computed against whatever legacy currently holds, and it runs after the response has gone out. If legacy state differs, or `forceAllowCreate` or validation behave differently, legacy ends up with a different object than unified storage. This divergence is not detected or logged.

Legacy write errors are no longer logged; failures in the goroutines are invisible

The old code logged legacy failures (`unable to create object in legacy storage`, `could not delete from legacy store`, `could not update object in legacy store`). In the new goroutines the error is only used as a boolean for `recordLegacyDuration`, and never logged. Combined with the cancelled-context problem, legacy writes can fail with no log trace. That makes legacy/unified divergence hard to diagnose. Log the error inside each goroutine.

Mode 3 integration runs reuse tests that read legacy immediately after k8s writes, but legacy writes are async

`doPlaylistTests` creates, updates and deletes through the k8s API and then immediately reads the legacy `/api/playlists` endpoint (`searchResponse`, `getFromBothAPIs`). In mode 3 the legacy write is fire-and-forget, so those assertions race with the goroutine. They are flaky, or they pass only by accident of timing. Mode 3 needs its own assertions, or the legacy checks should poll with `Eventually`.

Same `obj` is handed to the async legacy Create while the handler may still serialize `created`

The goroutine passes the original `obj` to `d.Legacy.Create` after `Storage.Create` has returned. `created` is often the same pointer or shares its internals with `obj`. Legacy Create commonly mutates the object (UID, resourceVersion, metadata), while the request handler concurrently encodes `created` for the response. This is an unsynchronized read/write on the same object (a data race). Deep-copy the object before launching the goroutine.

Storage create failure is recorded as a legacy duration metric

When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)`. The failure came from unified storage, so it should be `recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`. As written, storage errors pollute the legacy error and latency series and the storage error series stays empty, which misleads dashboards and alerts during the mode 3 rollout.

Storage update failure is recorded with recordLegacyDuration

On `d.Storage.Update` error the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` with `startStorage`. This is the same copy/paste mistake as in Create. Unified-storage failures get attributed to the legacy metric. It should be `recordStorageDuration`.

Unit tests never verify the asynchronous legacy writes

The Mode 3 tests only check the return values from unified storage. The legacy write runs in an un-awaited goroutine, and nothing asserts that Legacy.Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection are called, or that the legacy error path is handled. Because legacy and storage mocks share one `mock.Mock`, the legacy goroutine silently consumes the storage expectation. The tests would still pass if the goroutines were removed, or if they received a cancelled context. The tests need a sync mechanism (channel/WaitGroup or `Eventually`) with `AssertCalled`, and separate legacy and storage mocks.

Unrelated and duplicated go.work.sum entries

The go.work.sum changes (azure sdk, otel, alertmanager, genproto, etc.) are unrelated to the dual-writer change. The line for `github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery v0.0.0-20240701135906-559738ce6ae1/go.mod` is added twice, directly under the identical existing line. This looks like an accidental `go work sync` artifact and should be dropped from the PR.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
No re-check of the cache after taking the write lock

The cache is read under RLock, the lock is released, and then the write lock is taken without checking the cache again. At startup, or whenever the cache is nil, every concurrent caller sees nil. Each one then queues on `Lock()` and re-reads and re-parses assets-manifest.json one after another, even though the first caller has already filled the cache. In Dev mode every request takes the exclusive lock and does file I/O while holding it (and potentially an HTTP fetch if the CDN branch is enabled), which serializes all callers. A second check of `entryPointAssetsCache != nil && cfg.Env != setting.Dev` right after `Lock()` would avoid the redundant reloads.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

false_positives.candidate:
No regression test for the data race

The PR fixes a data race but adds no test. A test that calls `GetWebAssets` from many goroutines, run under `go test -race`, would show the race is fixed and stop it coming back. The package has no such coverage, so a later change to the cache logic could silently reintroduce the race.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enableSqlExpressions is a hard-coded `false` that ignores the feature flag

`enabled := !IsEnabledGlobally(FlagSqlExpressions); if enabled { return false }; return false` returns false on every path. The `sqlExpressions` toggle is now a no-op: enabling it changes nothing. The double negation and duplicated `return false` suggest the logic was gutted from a real flag check, so a future reader may think the flag still gates something. It also dereferences `h.features` for no effect, so a reader built with nil features would panic on an SQL query. Since the feature is intentionally off, return the error directly and drop the pointless flag lookup. Alternatively, document that the flag is now inert and fix its registry description.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.

false_positives.candidate:
No tests cover the new disabled behavior; existing SQL tests need updating

The PR replaces the DuckDB-backed implementation with stubs that always return "not implemented", and adds a reader gate that always rejects SQL queries, with no tests. Nothing asserts that `QueryTypeSQL` is rejected, or that `NewSQLCommand`, `TablesList` and `Execute` fail closed. Any existing tests (for example in `pkg/expr/sql` and `pkg/expr`) that exercise successful SQL parsing or execution can no longer pass. They should be skipped or removed explicitly rather than left failing or silently untouched. A regression test for the security-relevant gate is also missing.

Other SQL entry point reports a misleading error and is only blocked by the stub

The disable check lives only in `ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery`. `UnmarshalSQLCommand` and `NewSQLCommand` have no gate, so the legacy node-building path is blocked only because the stubbed `TablesList` returns "not implemented". That path then logs a Warn "invalid sql query", including the full user SQL, and returns "error reading SQL command" (`sql-invalid-sql`). Callers are told their SQL is invalid when the feature is disabled. Failing closed here is good, but the two entry points give inconsistent errors, and the security property depends on the stub rather than an explicit check. Put the disabled check in `NewSQLCommand` too, so all paths behave the same.

User-facing error text "sqlExpressions is not implemented" is misleading

SQL expressions were deliberately disabled for a security fix, and the feature flag still exists and is documented. Users who enable the flag now get "sqlExpressions is not implemented", which looks like a missing feature or a bug. The message should say the feature is disabled, preferably with a pointer to the CVE or advisory. The flag's registry description and docs still advertise SQL expressions and should be updated or marked as non-functional.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the BuildIndex lock allows duplicate concurrent builds of the same index

The old `cacheMu.Lock()` held for the whole of `BuildIndex` did more than serialize writes. `GetIndex` takes `RLock`, so it blocked while any build was running, and a second caller then found the freshly cached index. After this change `GetIndex` returns nil while a build is in progress. `searchSupport.getOrCreateIndex` (Search requests and the watch-event handler) can therefore start a second `BuildIndex` for the same key, and the search code has only a TODO about this. For file-backed indexes the second `bleve.New(dir, ...)` hits an existing path and fails, so the search errors or the watch event is dropped. For memory indexes the work is duplicated, the `IndexTenants` and `IndexedKinds` metrics are double-counted, and the first index is overwritten in the cache without being closed. A per-key singleflight or in-progress map is needed once the global lock is gone.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs iterates the cache map without taking cacheMu

`TotalDocs` ranges over `b.cache` without `RLock`, while `BuildIndex` now writes to the map under `Lock` from many goroutines with no other serialization. This PR adds a `TotalDocs()` call at the end of `searchSupport.init`, after the watch goroutine has already started. A watch event that triggers a lazy build of another index can therefore write the map while it is being iterated. Go's runtime treats that as a fatal 'concurrent map iteration and map write', which kills the process. `TotalDocs` should take `cacheMu.RLock()`.

false_positives.candidate:
Data race on shared `err` and `totalBatchesIndexed` in parallel index init

The errgroup goroutines in `init` increment the captured `totalBatchesIndexed` and assign to the outer `err` (`_, _, err = s.build(...)`) with no synchronization. With `WorkerThreads > 1`, which is the case this PR optimizes, this is a data race. A worker can also `return err` after another worker has overwritten the shared variable. A failed build can then be reported as nil, so startup init silently succeeds with a missing index, or it reports another goroutine's error. Now that init runs at startup this path always executes. Use a local `err` inside the closure and `atomic.Int64` for the counter.

Failed eager Init leaks the cancelable context and any started goroutines

When `s.Init(ctx)` fails, `NewResourceServer` returns `nil, err` without calling `cancel()` or `lifecycle.Stop`. By then `lifecycle.Init` may have succeeded and `search.init` may have started its event-watching goroutine, so those resources leak. Previously the server object stayed reachable and could be stopped. Call `cancel()` and best-effort `lifecycle.Stop` on the error path. The error is also logged twice, once inside `Init` and once here.

Requests are no longer rejected after Stop or a failed init

`Stop` sets `s.initErr` to 'service is stopping' or 'service is stopped'. This worked because every handler called `s.Init(ctx)`, which returns `s.initErr` after the `sync.Once`. With those calls removed, nothing reads `initErr` any more. After `Stop`, Create, Update, Delete, Read, List, Watch, Search and the blob endpoints keep running against a stopped backend and a cancelled server context. `IsHealthy` also no longer reports an unhealthy state when the server is stopping. Either keep a cheap stopped check in the handlers or drop the dead `initErr` writes in `Stop`.

Test skipped for postgres instead of investigating the startup-init regression

The test is skipped for postgres with 'not working with postgres in Drone'. It exercises the storage-server target, which now runs `ResourceServer.Init` synchronously at construction: backend DB init, index build and watcher start. A test that starts failing in CI right after eager init was introduced is a strong sign of a startup ordering or DB-readiness problem, such as tables or migrations not being ready when the server is built. Skipping it hides that signal, and the 'works locally' claim is unverified. No new test covers the changed behaviors: `NewResourceServer` failing on an init error, the index being built before the server is returned, or the lifecycle/search/watcher ordering.

Trace context propagation fix is incomplete

The PR is described as fixing trace propagation, but only `GetResourceStats` was changed to keep the span context. `WriteEvent` here still does `_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, ...)`. The same applies to `ReadResource` and `ListIterator` in this file and to `bleveBackend.BuildIndex` in bleve.go. The child spans (create/update/delete, the list queries, the bleve index writes) are parented to the caller's span instead of the new one, so traces are still flattened or mis-parented. Use `ctx, span :=` in these places as well.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup registers removal of a literal IDP "alias" instead of the created IDPs

`getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove)` binds to an IDP with the literal alias "alias", not the `idp-alias-N` IDPs just created. The same mistake is at line 425 for `idp-alias-20`, and the new test copied it from `testCacheIDPByOrg`. The cleanup never removes the 21 IDPs and will probably hit a 404 for the nonexistent "alias" when it runs. The test asserts exact counts, so leftover IDPs would make it order-dependent if the realm is not re-imported between tests. The variable alias should be captured, for example `testRealm().identityProviders().get(alias)::remove`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

false_positives.candidate:
No test for the positive invalidation paths of create/remove, or for the bean and org-disabled behaviour

`testCacheIDPForLogin` covers only creating or removing IDPs that are not login-eligible, which must not invalidate. It never creates or removes an IDP that is login-eligible, though `create()` and `remove()` now call `registerIDPLoginInvalidation` to invalidate in that case. It also does not cover disabled orgs, where the cache holds IDs based on raw DB state but `getById` returns wrapped models. The `isEnabled()` re-check added to `OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean` has no test either. The cached results are never compared with what `getForLogin` actually returns.

Update invalidation tests the org-wrapped `original` model, so its `isEnabled()` depends on org state and can skip a needed invalidation

`registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate` receives `original` from `getById()`. With the ORGANIZATION feature on, that is the wrapped model whose `isEnabled()` also requires the organization to exist and be enabled. The cached `getForLogin` ID sets are built from the raw DB state and ignore org enabled-state. If an IDP is linked to a disabled org, is enabled and public in the DB, and is already in the cached set, `test(original)` is false. An update that hides it on login, marks it link-only or disables it makes `test(updated)` false too, so the method returns early and nothing is invalidated. The stale ID set keeps the IDP. When the org is re-enabled, `getForLogin` returns the fresh model through `getById`. The bean in this PR re-checks only `isEnabled()`, not `hideOnLogin` or `linkOnly`, so an IDP that was hidden or link-only appears on the login page. The comparison should use the raw persisted state, for example the delegate's model or one not wrapped by the org-aware `isEnabled`.

remove() now always queries the DB for the IDP, even when it is in the cache

`idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias)` is now called unconditionally at the top of `remove()`. Previously the delegate was queried only when the alias key was invalidated; otherwise the cached entry supplied the internal id. The `else` branch's cache lookup no longer saves a query. The cached or already-loaded model could be used to decide whether login caches need invalidation.

true_positives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dead code: two ASN1Encoder results are computed and discarded

`ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` build encoders whose results are never used. The same values are encoded again in the `writeDerSeq(...)` call below. These look like leftover debugging lines and should be removed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract order() breaks every existing CryptoProvider implementation

order() is added to the public SPI interface as an abstract method. Any third-party or custom CryptoProvider compiled against the previous interface now fails to compile. A pre-compiled one throws AbstractMethodError, and CryptoIntegration.detectProvider calls order() during sorting, so startup fails. A default method (for example returning a neutral value) would add the ordering feature without breaking the contract.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

false_positives.candidate:
Multiple crypto providers no longer fail fast; ties at order 200 are resolved silently by classpath order

The old check threw IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was on the classpath. It is replaced with a sort by order() descending, taking the first, and logging the ignored ones only at debug level. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return 200. If, for example, both the default and FIPS providers end up on the classpath, the choice is decided only by ServiceLoader/classpath order. The server can then start in non-FIPS mode (or the reverse) without any warning. The ordering is meant to let the lower-order authz-client provider yield to a real one. Ties between real providers should still be an error, or at least be logged at warn. The ignored-providers message is also passed to debugf as the format string and ends with a dangling ", ".

Provider auto-selected by AuthzClient.create throws UnsupportedOperationException for core JCA operations

AuthzClient.create() now calls CryptoIntegration.init, which on a standalone client classpath selects this provider. Most of its methods (getSignature, getKeyFactory, getKeyPairGen, getX509CertFactory, getCertStore, getCertPathBuilder, getAesCbcCipher, getAesGcmCipher, getSecretKeyFact, getPemUtils, wrapFactoryForTruststore, ...) just throw UnsupportedOperationException. They could trivially delegate to the plain JDK (for example `Signature.getInstance(JavaAlgorithm.getJavaAlgorithm(alg))`, `KeyFactory.getInstance`). Keycloak core code paths that go through the CryptoProvider, such as signing client-assertion JWTs with an RSA/EC key or loading certificates and PEM keys, will fail at runtime with an unchecked exception. Only the ECDSA conversion helpers and getKeyStore are implemented.

Round-trip-only test cannot catch a symmetric encoder/decoder bug and does not use realistic curve sizes

The test only asserts that DER → R||S → DER → R||S returns the same R||S. It never checks that the re-encoded DER (`asn1Des`) equals the original JDK signature (`sign`). It never verifies the converted signature against the public key. A symmetric error in the custom ASN1Encoder/ASN1Decoder (for example non-minimal integer encoding or sign handling) would still pass. The key pair is always the default P-256 curve, even for ES384/ES512, so the 48- and 66-byte component paths are not exercised with matching keys. No negative or malformed-input cases are covered either. Adding `assertArrayEquals(sign, asn1Des)` and per-curve key generation would make the test meaningful.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.

Stale resources and permissions accumulate and show up when permissions are listed. The change also silently drops the previous behaviour in realms where neither feature is enabled. In `AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource`, per-client resources are created without a type, so they are not returned by `findByType`. The only resource with type `Clients` is the all-clients resource, whose name is the literal string "Clients", not a client id. If an all-clients permission grants the scope, the result is {"Clients"}, which matches no client. Clients granted individually are never returned. true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

false_positives.candidate:
Javadoc for requireView() and requireViewClientScopes() says "Returns true" but they are void and throw

`requireView()` (lines 95-98) and `requireViewClientScopes()` (lines 100-103) are documented as "Returns {@code true} if canView()/canViewClientScopes() returns true". Both methods are `void` and throw ForbiddenException when the check fails. Every other `require*` method in this same interface is documented correctly as "Throws ForbiddenException if ...". These two should be fixed to match.

No coverage for several new V2 client paths

The new tests cover manage, configure, view and map-roles(+composite) on clients. There is no test for `MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE`. Nothing checks that a client with a CONFIGURE or VIEW permission still cannot be managed or modified beyond what is intended. `getClientsWithPermission` and the client-scope management permissions (`canManageClientScopes`, `canView(ClientScopeModel)`) are not exercised either. The `getClientsWithPermission` path is the one with the likely defects noted above, and a test would have exposed them.

Test regenerates the secret of the client used to authenticate the admin client and mutates shared state without restoring it

`realmAdminClient` authenticates with client `myclient` and secret `mysecret`. `testConfigureOnlyOneClient` calls `clientResource.generateNewSecret()` on that same client. Once the secret is rotated, any later token acquisition or refresh by this admin client in the class (the token expires, or another test builds a new session) fails with 401 using the old secret. This makes the suite order- and timing-dependent. Other tests also leave persistent changes: they rename `myclient` and `realmClient`, move a default client scope to optional, and create roles on `myclient`. `onAfter` only removes permissions, so these mutations leak into subsequent tests.

Up to five full policy evaluations per client in canView(client) when listing

`canView(client)` calls `canView()` (one evaluation on the all-clients resource), then `canConfigure(client)`. That calls `canManage(client)` (a second evaluation) and a CONFIGURE `hasPermission` (a third). Finally it calls `hasPermission(client, VIEW)` (a fourth). Each `hasPermission` does a resource lookup, possibly a policy-store lookup, and a full `evaluatePermission` over all of the resource's scopes. Only one scope is inspected afterwards. When listing clients this runs per client, so cost grows quickly with realm size. Evaluating once and checking several scopes, or passing only the requested scope to the evaluation, would avoid the repetition.

canView() ignores an all-clients MANAGE grant while canView(ClientScopeModel) honours it

`canView()` is `canViewClientDefault() || hasPermission(VIEW)`. An admin with only the all-clients MANAGE scope therefore fails `canView()`/`requireView()`. `canView(ClientScopeModel)` explicitly accepts `VIEW || MANAGE`, and `canView(ClientModel)` accepts manage indirectly through `canConfigure`. For users, the tests treat manage as implying view. Endpoints guarded by the no-arg `canView()`/`requireView()` will behave differently from per-client and client-scope checks for the same admin.

getResourceName does not handle the Clients resource type

`getResourceName` special-cases only `USERS` ("All users" for the type resource, the username for a per-user resource). For a policy whose resourceType is `Clients`, it falls through to `resource.getDisplayName()`. Per-client resources are created in `getOrCreateResource` via `resourceStore.create(server, name, owner)` with no display name, and their name is the client's internal UUID. So the "all clients" resource and each per-client resource resolve to a null or opaque name when permissions are rendered. Clients need the same handling: "All clients" for the type resource and the clientId for a specific client.

The `null` case of testImageChange and testCacheMaxCount therefore runs without the feature in the CR. The test neither verifies this nor matches it, and the image-level flag makes the CR-level setting redundant. A regression in how the feature gets enabled would not be caught. The `check` subcommand has the same guard and no disabled-feature test. A regression that exits with 0 or 1, or drops the early return in `check`, would pass. Add assertions that the exit code is 4 for both subcommands. Also cover the renumbered RECREATE exit code (now 3) in testWrongVersions.

Macro hard-codes `--features=rolling-updates`, conflicting with the "use all your start options" instruction

The updatecompatibility macro appends a fixed `--features=rolling-updates` to every rendered example. The guide tells users to pass all the options they use with `start`, including `--features=...` in most real deployments. Following both instructions yields two `--features` options. Picocli rejects that or silently overrides one. Either way the metadata is computed against a different feature set than the running server, which is the case the warning in the guide describes. The guide should say that `rolling-updates` must be added to the existing feature list, rather than showing it as an extra standalone flag.

true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
V2 canManage() grants global group management for the VIEW scope

`canManage()` falls back to `hasPermission(null, VIEW, MANAGE)`, so a view-only permission on the "all groups" resource is enough to pass it. This is the check behind `GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup` (`auth.groups().requireManage()`). An admin who was granted only `view` on all groups can therefore create top-level groups. The per-group `canManage(GroupModel)` correctly uses only `MANAGE`, and the V1 equivalent requires the manage-users role, so this looks like a copy-paste from `canView()`. The Javadoc in `GroupPermissionEvaluator` repeats the same wrong contract. No test covers a VIEW-only admin attempting a manage operation. Change the call to `hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)`.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission uses resource IDs where group IDs (resource names) are needed

In V2 the authorization resource for a group is named after the group ID (see `AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup`, and `hasPermission` looks it up with `resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId)`). The callback here passes `groupResource.getId()`, which is the resource's own UUID, to `hasPermission`. That lookup by name never matches, so evaluation silently falls back to the generic "Groups" type resource and ignores the per-group permission. The method then adds `groupResource.getId()` to the result set, but callers (`UsersResource.searchForUser`, `getUsersCount`, `BruteForceUsersResource`) treat the values as group IDs for `UserModel.GROUPS` and `getUsersCount(..., groupIds)`. The result is wrong or empty sets and wrong user counts. For searches, the group restriction is not applied in the query, so the later per-user `canView` filter runs after `first`/`max` pagination and returns short or empty pages. The new test only checks the unpaginated search, where the post-filter hides the problem. Use `groupResource.getName()` for both the evaluation and the result, and skip the type-level resource whose name is "Groups".

false_positives.candidate:
Incorrect Javadoc on requireManageMembers and getGroupIdsWithViewPermission

The Javadoc for `requireManageMembers` says it throws when `canManageMembership(GroupModel)` returns false, but it actually delegates to `canManageMembers`. The Javadoc for `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission` says it returns a "Stream of IDs" while the method returns `Set<String>`. The `canManage()` Javadoc documents VIEW as sufficient for manage, which is wrong behavior (see the canManage finding above). Fix these descriptions.

`getResourceTypeResource` returns null when the "Groups" resource has not been created. This happens for realms whose admin-permissions client was initialized before this change, because `AdminPermissionsSchema.init` returns early when the client already exists and never adds the group scopes or resource. It also returns null if the schema is not active. The code passes that null straight into `policyStore.findByResource(server, resource)`, which throws an NPE and turns every group permission check into a 500. Add a null check and return false.

`testManageGroupMembership` only checks that `joinGroup` does not throw. It does not verify that bob became a member, and it has no negative case such as a different group without the permission. With thousands of message files and keys, a maintainer cannot tell which file or key failed from this message. The 'Illegal HTML' message does include both. When they do, `value.substring(start, value.length() - end)` has start > end and throws. Example: the English source has HTML, and the translation contains an unclosed `

Lithuanian login file now contains an Italian string for loginTotpStep1

true_positives.golden_comment: In AccessTokenContext constructor, the fourth Objects.requireNonNull validates grantType twice instead of validating rawTokenId, allowing null rawTokenId values to pass validation.

The encoded ID is `ssttgg:uuid`, so the grant shortcut is at indexes 4..6 (`substring(4, 6)`). The matcher uses `substring(3, 5)`, which spans the last char of the token type and the first char of the grant. It then does `if (...equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;`, which rejects a match instead of a mismatch. The two mistakes cancel out: the check can never fail, so `expectCodeToToken`, `expectDeviceCodeToToken`, `expectRefresh` and `expectAuthReqIdToToken` only verify the `xxxx:<uuid>` shape. If a grant type put the wrong shortcut in the token ID, the tests would still pass. Fix by comparing `items[0].substring(4, 6)` and returning false when it does NOT equal the expected shortcut. true_positives.golden_comment: Javadoc mentions "usually like 3-letters shortcut" but some implementations use 2-letter shortcuts ("ac", "cc", "rt", "te", "pc", "ci", "ro"). Consider updating documentation to reflect actual usage pattern.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Javadoc says 3-letter shortcut, but implementation requires exactly 2 characters

The Javadoc says the shortcut is 'usually like 3-letters', yet all factories use 2-letter shortcuts and the decoder (`encodedContext.length() != 6`, fixed 2-char slices) only works with exactly 2 characters. Someone implementing a custom grant following the Javadoc and using 3 letters would produce token IDs that cannot be parsed. The contract should state 'exactly 2 characters'.

true_positives.golden_comment: Catching generic RuntimeException is too broad. The implementation throws IllegalArgumentException specifically - catch that instead for more precise testing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
testIncorrectGrantType passes because of a NullPointerException, not the intended validation

In `before()`, the factory's `sessionFactory` is never set (it stays null). Decoding `ofrtac:5678` misses "ac" in `grantsByShortcuts`. `getGrantTypeByShortcut` then falls into the 'refresh maps' branch and calls `sessionFactory.getProviderFactoriesStream(...)`, which throws an NPE. The test catches any `RuntimeException`, so it passes on that NPE rather than on the `IllegalArgumentException` the decoder is supposed to throw for an unknown grant type. The test does not verify the real behavior. It should catch `IllegalArgumentException` specifically and provide a usable session factory, or the refresh fallback should be made testable.

false_positives.candidate:
Access token `jti` format change is user-visible but undocumented

Access token IDs (`jti`, also logged in the `token_id` event detail) change from a plain UUID to `<6-char context>:<uuid>`. Clients, log pipelines, or custom extensions that assume the `jti` is a UUID will behave differently. This PR adds no release/upgrade note or documentation for the new format or the new `tokenContextEncoder` SPI, so operators have no notice of the change.

Access token is tagged ONLINE even when the session is converted to offline right after

The session type is derived from `userSession.isOffline()` at access-token creation time. In authorization-code and ROPC flows with `offline_access`, the access token is created first from the online user session. Only afterwards does `generateRefreshToken()` create the offline session, and the online session is then removed (`FIRST_OFFLINE_ACCESS` and ROPC handling in `OAuth2GrantTypeBase`/`ResourceOwnerPasswordCredentialsGrantType`). That access token gets an `on` prefix, but its `sid` points to a session that no longer exists as online, and only the offline session remains. The stated purpose of the PR is to let endpoints look up only the correct session type. For these tokens the encoded session type would point at the wrong (non-existent) session type. The offline_access case should be considered when computing the session type, or the limitation should at least be documented.

Grant shortcuts are not validated (null or length != 2)

`postInit` inserts `gtf.getShortcut()` into a `ConcurrentHashMap` without validating it. A third-party `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` returning null causes an NPE during server startup. A shortcut that is not exactly 2 chars makes tokens encode fine, but `getTokenContextFromTokenId` then throws `IllegalArgumentException` because it requires the context part to be exactly 6 chars. The existing duplicate check only covers collisions, and the lazy refresh paths in `getShortcutByGrantType`/`getGrantTypeByShortcut` skip validation too. Add an explicit startup check that every shortcut is non-null and exactly 2 characters, with a clear error message.

New abstract method breaks existing OAuth2GrantTypeFactory implementations

`getShortcut()` is added as an abstract method to a provider SPI interface. Any custom grant type factory compiled against the previous version fails to compile and, if already built, throws `AbstractMethodError` when `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit` calls it. Since the encoder already has an 'na' fallback, a default implementation would keep existing extensions working. If it is intentionally mandatory, this breaking change should be called out in the upgrade notes.

true_positives.golden_comment: After creating the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel, consider setting its id from the stored credential (e.g., myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()); otherwise getId() will be null and downstream removal by id (e.g., removeStoredCredentialById in the authenticator flow) may not work.

User-storage recovery codes are never consumed, so they can be replayed and the same code is always requested

`isValid` for recovery codes only checks that the submitted code is in the stored JSON list and never marks it used. `getCredentials` (line ~237) rebuilds a fresh `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues(...)` from the full list on every call, so every code always looks unused. `RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean` therefore always asks for the same code number (index 0). Any code stays valid indefinitely, which breaks the one-time semantics of the local provider. The `allCodesUsed()` cleanup in `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator` can never trigger for federated credentials. The new model also has no id, because `createFromValues` does not carry over `recoveryCodes.getId()`, so `removeStoredCredentialById(model.getId())` would be called with a null id if it were ever reached. Creating codes in user storage leaves stale local recovery codes valid (and vice versa)

When `updateCredential` succeeds, the method returns without touching any existing recovery-codes credential in the local DB. The local `createCredential` path likewise ignores federated codes. If a user already has local recovery codes and the storage later accepts the type, regenerating codes in the storage does not invalidate the old local ones. `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential` prefers the federated credential while `isValid` can still accept the old local codes. The user then holds two live recovery-code sets, and regenerating codes does not revoke the previous set.

Recovery codes can be created and validated in user storage but not disabled or removed

`supportsCredentialType`, `updateCredential`, `isConfiguredFor` and `isValid` now handle recovery codes. `getDisableableCredentialTypesStream` and `disableCredentialType` still only handle OTP. An admin therefore cannot see recovery codes as a disableable credential, and `disableCredentialType` logs "Unsupported to disable credential" and does nothing. Once recovery codes are written to the user storage they can never be removed through the admin API, which is inconsistent with the OTP handling next to it.

Recovery-key test covers only one happy-path login

`testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin` sets up codes and logs in once with code index 0. It does not test a wrong code being rejected, a second login that should ask for the next code index, reuse of an already-used code, or the exhausted-codes path (`allCodesUsed` removal and re-adding the required action). The first two would have exposed that user-storage codes are never consumed. The flow also includes a pointless `delayed-authenticator` with a constant `delay` of 0 and a misspelled alias (`delayed-suthenticator-config`), which looks copy-pasted from another test.

Undocumented SPI contract: plaintext JSON list of codes handed to user storage

`createRecoveryCodesCredential` serializes the raw (unhashed) recovery codes to a JSON array and passes them as the value of a `UserCredentialModel`. The local provider stores only hashes. The javadoc says nothing about this format, that the storage receives plaintext codes, or how the storage should report used/unused codes through `getCredentials` (see the replay problem above). Third-party `CredentialInputUpdater` implementations have to guess the contract, and storing plaintext codes is a security-relevant decision that should be stated. The provider id is also hard-coded as `"keycloak-recovery-authn-codes"` instead of using the factory constant.

getCredentials dereferences a possibly-null MyUser

`getMyUser(user)` returns null when the username is not in the `users` map, for example after `removeUser` or for a user from another provider instance. `getCredentials` then calls `myUser.recoveryCodes` immediately and throws an NPE. Every other method in this class (`isConfiguredFor`, `isValid`, `getDisableableCredentialTypesStream`) guards against null. Since `getFederatedCredentialsStream()` is now called from the login path via `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential`, this can turn a missing user into a 500.

When the backing group no longer exists, `getSubGroupsCount()` returns `null` instead of failing. The `GroupModel` contract does not document a null result. The callback here passes `groupResource.getId()`, which is the resource's own UUID, to `hasPermission`. The method then adds `groupResource.getId()` to the result set, but callers (`UsersResource.searchForUser`, `getUsersCount`, `BruteForceUsersResource`) treat the values as group IDs for `UserModel.GROUPS` and `getUsersCount(..., groupIds)`. Weak and missing assertions in group permission tests

`testManageGroupMembership` only checks that `joinGroup` does not throw. It does not verify that bob became a member, and it has no negative case such as a different group without the permission. The test suite also has no case showing that a VIEW-only permission on all groups cannot create or modify groups, which would have caught the `canManage()` bug. true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract order() breaks every existing CryptoProvider implementation

order() is added to the public SPI interface as an abstract method. Any third-party or custom CryptoProvider compiled against the previous interface now fails to compile. A pre-compiled one throws AbstractMethodError, and CryptoIntegration.detectProvider calls order() during sorting, so startup fails. A default method (for example returning a neutral value) would add the ordering feature without breaking the contract.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same issue: adding an abstract `order()` method to the `CryptoProvider` interface breaks backward compatibility with existing implementations.

false_positives.candidate:
Multiple crypto providers no longer fail fast; ties at order 200 are resolved silently by classpath order

The old check threw IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was on the classpath. It is replaced with a sort by order() descending, taking the first, and logging the ignored ones only at debug level. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return 200. If, for example, both the default and FIPS providers end up on the classpath, the choice is decided only by ServiceLoader/classpath order. The server can then start in non-FIPS mode (or the reverse) without any warning. The ordering is meant to let the lower-order authz-client provider yield to a real one. Ties between real providers should still be an error, or at least be logged at warn. The ignored-providers message is also passed to debugf as the format string and ends with a dangling ", ".

Provider auto-selected by AuthzClient.create throws UnsupportedOperationException for core JCA operations

AuthzClient.create() now calls CryptoIntegration.init, which on a standalone client classpath selects this provider. Most of its methods (getSignature, getKeyFactory, getKeyPairGen, getX509CertFactory, getCertStore, getCertPathBuilder, getAesCbcCipher, getAesGcmCipher, getSecretKeyFact, getPemUtils, wrapFactoryForTruststore, ...) just throw UnsupportedOperationException. They could trivially delegate to the plain JDK (for example `Signature.getInstance(JavaAlgorithm.getJavaAlgorithm(alg))`, `KeyFactory.getInstance`). Keycloak core code paths that go through the CryptoProvider, such as signing client-assertion JWTs with an RSA/EC key or loading certificates and PEM keys, will fail at runtime with an unchecked exception. Only the ECDSA conversion helpers and getKeyStore are implemented.

Round-trip-only test cannot catch a symmetric encoder/decoder bug and does not use realistic curve sizes

The test only asserts that DER → R||S → DER → R||S returns the same R||S. It never checks that the re-encoded DER (`asn1Des`) equals the original JDK signature (`sign`). It never verifies the converted signature against the public key. A symmetric error in the custom ASN1Encoder/ASN1Decoder (for example non-minimal integer encoding or sign handling) would still pass. The key pair is always the default P-256 curve, even for ES384/ES512, so the 48- and 66-byte component paths are not exercised with matching keys. No negative or malformed-input cases are covered either. Adding `assertArrayEquals(sign, asn1Des)` and per-curve key generation would make the test meaningful.

true_positives.golden_comment: The reader thread isn’t waited for; flipping deletedAll to true and asserting immediately can race and miss exceptions added just after the flag change, making this test flaky.

The thread may be mid-request at that point, so an exception from the last iteration can be added after the assertion has already passed, which makes the test unreliable. The thread can also keep calling the admin client after the test ends and the realm is cleaned up. Keep a reference to the thread and `join()` it (with a timeout) before asserting. The loop also has no pacing, so it hammers the server with `Integer.MAX_VALUE` page sizes. Nothing guarantees the read overlaps the deletes, so the test may pass without ever exercising the race.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: the reader thread is never joined/waited for after setting `deletedAll` to true, leading to a race condition where exceptions occurring on the final iteration might be missed by the immediate assertion, making the test flaky.

The comment and method name say the test covers a user who has no passkey, but the test only disables passkeys at the realm level with `setWebAuthnPolicyPasskeysEnabled(FALSE)`. isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) is False for spawn processes, so hung flushers are never killed

The new `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` guard around `process.kill()` is therefore always False in production, and the kill never runs. The old code called `self.process.kill()` unconditionally. When the cause is `hang`, the stuck process is now left running and `_create_process_for_shards` starts a second flusher for the same shards. Two flushers then consume and produce the same segments concurrently, and every further restart leaks one more process. Use `hasattr(process, 'kill')` or check `multiprocessing.context.BaseProcess`/`SpawnProcess` instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join() never terminates spawned processes, and its deadline break skips cleanup for the rest

Two problems in `join()`. First, `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` is False for `SpawnProcess`, so `process.terminate()` never runs for real flusher processes. Second, the new `if remaining_time <= 0: break` leaves the loop before reaching terminate for the current and all remaining processes. If the deadline expires while waiting on an early process, the later processes are neither waited on nor terminated. Terminate should run for every process regardless of the deadline, and the type check needs to match `SpawnProcess`.

That method appears to report on the whole Redis cluster rather than just the buffer's shards. If so, each submit issues N times the INFO calls, and `used` and `available` are both inflated by N. The ratio stays the same, so the result is correct but wasteful. The same applies to `record_stored_segments` per buffer. Query memory once, from a single buffer.

age/timestamp mutual-exclusion check uses truthiness and is not enforced when both are missing

true_positives.golden_comment: Analytics events are recorded before the feature flag check, resulting in analytics being logged for all requests, including those that return 404 due to the feature being disabled. This can lead to misleading analytics data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Analytics event recorded before the feature-flag check

`analytics.record("preprod_artifact.api.assemble", ...)` runs before the `organizations:preprod-artifact-assemble` feature check. Requests from orgs without the feature (which get a 404) are still counted as assemble API usage, which skews the metric. Also, `request.user.id` is None for org-auth-token requests, so those events carry no user. Move the call after the feature check unless counting rejected requests is intended.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the exact same problem as the golden comment: analytics events are recorded before the feature flag check, causing 404 requests from organizations without the feature to skew the analytics metrics.

false_positives.candidate:
Error timestamps (seconds) compared against replay event timestamps (milliseconds)

`gen_request_data` interleaves errors with breadcrumbs by checking `error_events[idx]["timestamp"] < event.get("timestamp", 0)`. The error timestamp comes from the nodestore event payload, which is epoch seconds. The `event["timestamp"]` from an rrweb replay segment is normally epoch milliseconds. With real data every error then compares as 'earlier' than the first replay event, so all errors are emitted at the start of the log instead of in chronological order. The Seer summary receives a wrong timeline. The tests use the same unit for both sides (`now.timestamp()` for both, and small numbers in `test_get_request_data`), so they cannot catch this. Normalise the units, for example by multiplying the error timestamp by 1000, and add a test that uses millisecond replay timestamps.

Per-issue get_recommended_event() lookup when building PR comments

`get_environment_info` calls `issue.get_recommended_event()` for every issue in the comment (up to 5). That performs an event lookup (Snuba plus nodestore) per issue, synchronously in the comment-building path, just to show an environment name. Failures are swallowed and logged only at `info`, so persistent lookup problems will go unnoticed and the comment silently loses the environment. Consider a single batched lookup, or reading the environment from data already available on the group or query.

Issue title placed unescaped inside markdown link text and truncated mid-token

`MERGED_PR_SINGLE_ISSUE_TEMPLATE` puts the raw (user-controlled) issue title inside `[**{title}**]({url})`. A title containing `]`, `[`, `**` or `](...)` breaks the link or lets the title alter the rendered link in the PR comment. `_truncate_title` cuts at 50 characters without regard to markdown, so it can also leave an unbalanced `**` or bracket and mangle the rest of the comment. The title should be escaped, or have markdown-significant characters stripped, before it is interpolated.

Unknown report types reject the whole batch with 422

`type` is a `ChoiceField` limited to 8 values, and a single invalid report makes the endpoint return 422 for the entire array. The Reporting API can deliver other report types to a collector (e.g. `network-error` or newer types), and browsers batch reports. One report of an unlisted type discards all valid reports in the same request. The previous code only used the types as hints and accepted everything. For a data-collection endpoint it is safer to skip or tag unknown types than to fail the batch.

Default autofix automation tuning silently changed from 'low' to 'off'

`DEFAULT_AUTOFIX_AUTOMATION_TUNING_DEFAULT` and the `sentry:autofix_automation_tuning` project option default both change from `"low"` to `"off"`. Every project that never set the option explicitly changes behaviour on deploy: autofix automation turns off, and the API/serializer now reports `off`. This has nothing to do with the PR title (replay bulk delete), and the PR description is just 'Test 5'. It should be a separate, clearly described change, with a decision on whether existing projects need a migration to preserve their effective setting.

New max_segment_id=None handling is not actually exercised

The test now feeds `max_segment_id: None`, but it patches `delete_matched_rows`, so the real `_make_recording_filenames` / `delete_replay_recordings` code that gained the `None` early-return is never run. A regression back to `range(None + 1)` would still pass. Add a direct unit test of `_make_recording_filenames` with a `None` segment id, or an unmocked `delete_matched_rows` test.

60s processing deadline for a batch of up to 100 external identity refreshes

`check_auth_identities` loops over up to `chunk_size=100` auth identities. Each `check_single_auth_identity` makes a network call to the SSO provider's `refresh_identity`. A fixed `processing_deadline_duration=60` allows only about 0.6s per identity, so a slow provider can hit the deadline. `check_auth` has already bumped `last_synced` for the whole chunk, so the identities that were not reached will not be re-selected until the next interval (about a day). The final `check_auth.apply_async` reschedule is also skipped. Size the deadline to the chunk, or reduce the chunk size.

Query key omits organization; isLoading/attributes semantics changed

The react-query key is `['use-trace-item-attribute-keys', queryOptions]`, but `queryOptions` contains no organization slug, and the fetch URL does depend on `organization.slug`. Cached attribute keys can be reused across organizations within a session. The hook also now returns `isLoading: isFetching`, which is true on every background refetch rather than only the initial load. `attributes` can now be `undefined` (it was previously always a `TagCollection`). Callers that gate UI on `isLoading` or assume a defined object may flicker or break. The old `staleTime: 0`, `refetchOnWindowFocus: false` and `retry: false` options were also dropped.

Saved queries with multi-yAxis visualizes will always look modified

Every `work_queue.put()` then raises `queue.ShutDown`. `submit()` catches `Exception`, marks the offset as added and completed, and moves on. The result is that after the first rebalance every message is dropped without being processed, and its offset is still committed. The tracker also keeps `last_committed`, `all_offsets` and `outstanding` for partitions that were revoked or reassigned. The strategy should not own the shared pool's lifecycle.
