This can race with the main thread's own consumer calls. It can also commit offsets for partitions that have just been revoked, which makes `stage_offsets` raise. When that raise happens, `mark_committed` is skipped. The tracker never forgets the revoked partition, so the same failing commit is retried and logged every second indefinitely. Commits should be handed back to the main thread, for example by recording the committable offsets and calling `commit` from `poll()`.

Meanwhile no offsets are committed because commits are contiguous. `get_committable_offsets` walks `range(start, max_offset + 1)` and stops at the first offset that is not in `all_offsets`. After `mark_committed` trims the set, a single missing offset means `highest_committable` never advances past it. The consumer then stops committing for that partition forever, `all_offsets` grows without bound, and a restart replays everything since the gap. `test_offset_gaps_block_commits` encodes this behavior as desired. A safer approach is to track only the offsets actually submitted, in order, and commit up to the smallest outstanding offset.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes derive their context from the request context, which is cancelled when the handler returns

Each goroutine (Create l.51, Delete l.110, Update l.135, DeleteCollection l.163) does `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` on the request-scoped `ctx`. The API server cancels that context as soon as the HTTP handler returns, and the goroutine intentionally outlives the handler. The legacy write will therefore usually run with an already-cancelled context and fail or abort. The legacy store silently drifts from unified storage, which is the opposite of the 'safe measure' described in the PR. Use `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (or a fresh background context carrying the logger) as the parent of the timeout context.

Legacy write errors are no longer logged; failures in the goroutines are invisible

The old code logged legacy failures (`unable to create object in legacy storage`, `could not delete from legacy store`, `could not update object in legacy store`). In the new goroutines the error is only used as a boolean for `recordLegacyDuration`, and never logged. Combined with the cancelled-context problem, legacy writes can fail with no log trace. That makes legacy/unified divergence hard to diagnose. Log the error inside each goroutine.

Storage create failure is recorded as a legacy duration metric

When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)`. The failure came from unified storage, so it should be `recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`. As written, storage errors pollute the legacy error and latency series and the storage error series stays empty, which misleads dashboards and alerts during the mode 3 rollout.

Storage update failure is recorded with recordLegacyDuration

On `d.Storage.Update` error the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` with `startStorage`. This is the same copy/paste mistake as in Create. Unified-storage failures get attributed to the legacy metric. It should be `recordStorageDuration`.

Legacy DeleteCollection duration is recorded as a storage duration

Inside the goroutine that calls `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection`, the result is recorded with `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ..., startLegacy)`. It should be `recordLegacyDuration`. Legacy latency and errors are attributed to the storage metrics, which double-counts storage and hides legacy failures.

Legacy update re-applies the original objInfo instead of the object written to storage

The previous implementation wrapped the result in `updateWrapper` so legacy stored exactly the object that unified storage persisted. Now the goroutine calls `d.Legacy.Update(ctx, name, objInfo, ...)` with the raw `objInfo`. For patch/apply requests the update is re-computed against whatever legacy currently holds, and it runs after the response has gone out. If legacy state differs, or `forceAllowCreate` or validation behave differently, legacy ends up with a different object than unified storage. This divergence is not detected or logged.

Same `obj` is handed to the async legacy Create while the handler may still serialize `created`

The goroutine passes the original `obj` to `d.Legacy.Create` after `Storage.Create` has returned. `created` is often the same pointer or shares its internals with `obj`. Legacy Create commonly mutates the object (UID, resourceVersion, metadata), while the request handler concurrently encodes `created` for the response. This is an unsynchronized read/write on the same object (a data race). Deep-copy the object before launching the goroutine.

Unit tests never verify the asynchronous legacy writes

The Mode 3 tests only check the return values from unified storage. The legacy write runs in an un-awaited goroutine, and nothing asserts that Legacy.Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection are called, or that the legacy error path is handled. Because legacy and storage mocks share one `mock.Mock`, the legacy goroutine silently consumes the storage expectation. The tests would still pass if the goroutines were removed, or if they received a cancelled context. The tests need a sync mechanism (channel/WaitGroup or `Eventually`) with `AssertCalled`, and separate legacy and storage mocks.

Mode 3 integration runs reuse tests that read legacy immediately after k8s writes, but legacy writes are async

`doPlaylistTests` creates, updates and deletes through the k8s API and then immediately reads the legacy `/api/playlists` endpoint (`searchResponse`, `getFromBothAPIs`). In mode 3 the legacy write is fire-and-forget, so those assertions race with the goroutine. They are flaky, or they pass only by accident of timing. Mode 3 needs its own assertions, or the legacy checks should poll with `Eventually`.

The go.work.sum changes (azure sdk, otel, alertmanager, genproto, etc.) are unrelated to the dual-writer change. This looks like an accidental `go work sync` artifact and should be dropped from the PR.

If a key is missing in the user's locale, the fallback chain [locale, default, :en] finds nothing because :en may not be loaded in that process. The result is a 'translation missing: ...' string, not the English text. A fresh worker process hits this on its first email in a non-English locale. The loading belongs in the accelerator, for example `translate`/`load_locale` loading the whole fallback chain, not in one controller filter.

The cache key is `key + config.locale + backend.object_id`. With this PR the result also depends on `SiteSetting.default_locale` (the custom fallback chain) and on which fallback locales are already loaded. Two consequences follow. (1) If an admin changes the default locale, entries cached for other locales still hold text from the old fallback until they are evicted or the process restarts. (2) If a lookup runs before the fallback locales are loaded, the frozen 'translation missing' string is stored under that key. It is then served on every later call, even after :en has been loaded. The key should include the fallback chain, or the cache should be cleared when the default locale changes. Missing-translation results should not be cached.

Regressions in this globally applied behavior would go unnoticed.

false_positives.candidate:
raw_html posts are stored and rendered with no sanitization (stored XSS)

`Post#cook` returns `raw` verbatim when `cook_method == raw_html`, so none of the normal cooking or sanitizing pipeline runs. The content comes from remote sources. In `PollFeed` it is `CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content)`, which turns escaped entities such as `<script>` back into live markup. In `import_remote` it is the readability output. The result is written to `posts.cooked`, shown on the main site, and emitted via `<%= raw post.cooked %>` in the embed iframe, which is served from the Discourse origin with `X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL`. A compromised or malicious feed or page can therefore run script in Discourse's origin. The imported HTML should be sanitized with a whitelist before it is saved or served.

Wrapping PostCreator in Topic.transaction defeats its after-commit job enqueueing

`PostCreator#create` deliberately enqueues `process_post` and `feature_topic_users` after its own transaction commits (see the comment in `enqueue_jobs`). Wrapping the call in an outer `Topic.transaction` means those jobs are enqueued before the outer transaction commits, which now also includes `TopicEmbed.create!`. In production a Sidekiq worker can pick up `process_post` before the post row is visible and fail or skip processing. It also makes the rollback semantics unclear, because the `ActiveRecord::Rollback` raised inside PostCreator's nested transaction does not roll back the outer one.

Failed post creation is not detected before creating the TopicEmbed

`PostCreator#create` returns `@post` even when it failed and rolled back, for example on host-spam detection or a save failure. That post is unsaved, so `post.present?` is still true. `TopicEmbed.create!` then runs with `post_id: nil` and `topic_id: nil`, which raises a NOT NULL violation. This surfaces as a confusing exception in the job instead of a clean failure. The guard should check `post.persisted?` or `post.errors.blank?`. The update branch has a related problem: `embed.post` can be nil if the post was deleted, and `PostRevisor.new(nil)` then blows up.

`href.start_with?('/')` also matches protocol-relative links such as `//cdn.example.com/x.jpg`. `sub(/^\/+/, '')` strips both slashes, giving `http://host/cdn.example.com/x.jpg`, which is a broken link. The same happens for `img src` on line 71. Relative paths without a leading slash (`images/a.png`, `../a.png`) are left untouched, and the code resolves against only scheme and host rather than the article URL. The port check (`!= 80 && != 443`) is also wrong for https on 80 or http on 443. `URI.join(url, href)` handles all of these correctly.

Throttle is keyed on the full URL and non-atomic, so it is trivially bypassed

The key is `retrieved:#{@embed_url}`, so varying the query string (`?a=1`, `?a=2`, ...) on the allowed host gets a fresh throttle slot each time. Each one triggers a full `Jobs::PollFeed` run (fetch, parse and import of the whole feed) when feed polling is enabled, plus a remote HTTP fetch and a new topic via `import_remote`. This allows request amplification and duplicate topics per URL variant. The embed URL should be canonicalized, and there should be a global limit on retrievals. Separately, `setnx` followed by `expire` is not atomic. A crash between the two leaves a key that never expires and blocks that URL permanently. Use `SET key val NX EX 60`.

`create_table ..., force: true` runs `DROP TABLE` first if the table exists. Here it is in the new `topic_embeds` migration and in the edited `20131223171005_create_top_topics.rb`. The latter is an already-applied migration unrelated to this feature, and the edit has no effect except when the migration is re-run, when it silently destroys data. Each import now also performs a live HTTP fetch of the thread link, so the task fails or produces content from the live site if the link is dead. Unsubscribe toggle is not idempotent: reloading the page mutes the topic

The first visit drops a watching or tracking user to regular. Any later hit on the same URL, whether a page reload, a double click, or an email-client or security-scanner prefetch, sees `notification_level <= regular` and mutes the topic. A user who only asked to stop watching can end up with the topic fully muted. The resulting state depends on how many times the URL is requested, not on user intent. The action should be idempotent, or require explicit confirmation before escalating to muted.

State-changing action exposed on GET (CSRF / prefetch)

`get "t/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe"` and `get "t/:topic_id/unsubscribe"` map to an action that writes `topic_users.notification_level`. GET requests are not covered by CSRF protection. A post or any third-party page that embeds an image or link pointing at `/t/x/<id>/unsubscribe` will change the notification level for any logged-in viewer. Link prefetchers and scanners trigger it too. The write should be a POST/PUT from the client page (with a CSRF token) after the user confirms, rather than a side effect of loading the page.

The notification level is set by assigning the attribute and calling `tu.save!`. Everywhere else it is changed through `TopicUser.change`, which sets `notifications_changed_at` and `notifications_reason_id` (to `user_changed`) and publishes `notification_level_change` on MessageBus. Here the reason stays at its old value, the timestamp is not updated, and other open tabs are not told about the change. Use `TopicUser.change(current_user, topic_id, notification_level: ...)` to keep behaviour consistent.

The spec had to be edited to pass `unsubscribe_url` to avoid this. Provide a fallback in `template_args`, or only include the per-topic sentence when `unsubscribe_url` is present.

If it does not resolve, the unsubscribe page renders empty and shows neither the message nor the notification dropdown. The only spec change is adding `unsubscribe_url` to an existing fixture so it stops raising. Nothing asserts that the per-topic URL appears in the email body or HTML part. There is no controller spec for `TopicsController#unsubscribe`, covering downgrade to regular, escalation to muted, the slug redirect, the missing-TopicUser case and the not-logged-in case. There is no spec for `Topic#unsubscribe_url`. The behaviour problems above (nil TopicUser, non-idempotent toggle) would have been caught by basic controller tests.

Working-hours check is wrong: `end` equals `start`, and multiple ranges per day reject everything

false_positives.candidate:
Multiple date-override ranges on the same day make most slots unavailable

`dateOverrides.find(...)` returns true (slot rejected) as soon as ANY override range on that day does not contain the slot. A host with two override intervals on one date (e.g. 09:00-11:00 and 14:00-16:00) is a supported setup. A slot at 14:30 is outside the first interval, so `find` returns true on it and the slot is rejected even though it is inside the second. The check needs to pass when the slot fits in at least one same-day override, and fail only when it fits in none. As written, the new logic wrongly drops valid slots for fixed hosts, and for collective and loose hosts too, since all of them now go through this check.

Slots that only partially overlap a date override are treated as available

The override test only rejects a slot if `slotEnd <= override.start` or `slotStart > override.end`. A slot that starts before the override and ends inside it is accepted. A slot that starts inside the override and ends after `override.end` is accepted. A slot starting exactly at `override.end` is accepted, because `isAfter` is strict. Example: with a fixed-host override of 10:00-11:00, a 10:30-11:30 or 11:00-12:00 slot generated from another host's availability passes. This is the situation the PR is meant to prevent (RR events booked when the fixed host is unavailable). The condition should be that the whole slot lies in `[override.start, override.end]`, i.e. reject when `slotStart < start` or `slotEnd > end`.

Override-to-slot matching uses the UTC calendar day and breaks for overrides crossing UTC midnight

An override is matched to a slot only when the UTC date of the shifted `override.start` equals the UTC date of `slotStartTime`. For organizers far from UTC, an override that begins on one UTC day and ends on the next (e.g. 10:00-18:00 PST is 18:00-02:00 UTC) will not match slots falling on the second UTC day. Those slots are then treated as having no override and fall through to the normal working-hours/busy logic. This can wrongly allow or deny them, which defeats the override.

Timezone-shifted overrides can wrap past midnight and land on the wrong invitee day

The override is selected for an invitee day by `activeOverrides` using the unshifted (organizer-wall-clock-as-UTC) `override.start`. Only afterwards is the invitee-organizer offset added and reduced to `hour()*60+minute()`. Two problems follow. (1) If the shift pushes the start/end past midnight, the minutes wrap modulo 24h, so start or end becomes a small number and the range is either dropped (`start >= end` is skipped in `buildSlots`) or shown on the wrong day. (2) The day the override is attached to is computed before the shift. With a large timezone gap (e.g. organizer in Kolkata with a 20:00-23:00 override, invitee in Tokyo) the override can be attached to the day after the one it really falls on. The shifted instant, not the raw one, should be used for both the day filter and the minute-of-day computation.

`dayjs(override.start.toString())` goes through `Date.prototype.toString()`, which yields a locale/host-timezone formatted string without milliseconds that is re-parsed by the engine. None covers multiple override ranges on one day, slots overlapping an override boundary, or overrides crossing midnight or UTC midnight, which are exactly where the new logic is fragile. The added timezone test (Dhaka) only shifts by 30 minutes and expects identical UTC slots. The `toHaveTimeSlots` matcher also passes when the actual list is shorter than the expected list, so missing slots would go unnoticed.

The unchecked exception escapes the lambda in `verifySafeHtml`, so the build dies with a stack trace instead of the intended 'Illegal HTML in key ...' message. Null check for rawTokenId actually checks grantType

A null `rawTokenId` is accepted silently, and `encodeTokenId` would then emit a token ID ending in the literal string "null" (e.g. `onrtac:null`) instead of failing fast. It should be `requireNonNull(rawTokenId, ...)`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same constructor validation bug: the fourth Objects.requireNonNull checks grantType again rather than rawTokenId, allowing a null rawTokenId to pass. The candidate adds a consequence but points to the same issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: In isAccessTokenId, the substring for the grant shortcut and the equality check look inverted: the grant shortcut occupies indices 4–5 (substring(4,6)), and a match should return true (combined with UUID check), not false.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isAccessTokenId matcher never checks the grant shortcut (wrong offset and inverted condition)

The encoded ID is `ssttgg:uuid`, so the grant shortcut is at indexes 4..6 (`substring(4, 6)`). The matcher uses `substring(3, 5)`, which spans the last char of the token type and the first char of the grant. It then does `if (...equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;`, which rejects a match instead of a mismatch. The two mistakes cancel out: the check can never fail, so `expectCodeToToken`, `expectDeviceCodeToToken`, `expectRefresh` and `expectAuthReqIdToToken` only verify the `xxxx:<uuid>` shape. If a grant type put the wrong shortcut in the token ID, the tests would still pass. Fix by comparing `items[0].substring(4, 6)` and returning false when it does NOT equal the expected shortcut. The failure message in `describeTo` is also not meaningful.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug in isAccessTokenId: the grant shortcut substring uses the wrong indices and the equality check is inverted so a match returns false instead of true.

true_positives.golden_comment: Javadoc mentions "usually like 3-letters shortcut" but some implementations use 2-letter shortcuts ("ac", "cc", "rt", "te", "pc", "ci", "ro"). Consider updating documentation to reflect actual usage pattern.

true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same documentation/contract mismatch: the Javadoc describes shortcuts as usually 3 letters, while actual implementations and the decoder require exactly 2-character shortcuts. The candidate adds detail about parsing failure but points to the same underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: Catching generic RuntimeException is too broad. The implementation throws IllegalArgumentException specifically - catch that instead for more precise testing.

Decoding `ofrtac:5678` misses "ac" in `grantsByShortcuts`. `getGrantTypeByShortcut` then falls into the 'refresh maps' branch and calls `sessionFactory.getProviderFactoriesStream(...)`, which throws an NPE. The test catches any `RuntimeException`, so it passes on that NPE rather than on the `IllegalArgumentException` the decoder is supposed to throw for an unknown grant type. true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify that the test catches a generic RuntimeException and should instead catch IllegalArgumentException specifically. The candidate adds detail about an NPE masking the intended validation, but the core concern matches.

false_positives.candidate:
Access token is tagged ONLINE even when the session is converted to offline right after

The session type is derived from `userSession.isOffline()` at access-token creation time. In authorization-code and ROPC flows with `offline_access`, the access token is created first from the online user session. Only afterwards does `generateRefreshToken()` create the offline session, and the online session is then removed (`FIRST_OFFLINE_ACCESS` and ROPC handling in `OAuth2GrantTypeBase`/`ResourceOwnerPasswordCredentialsGrantType`). That access token gets an `on` prefix, but its `sid` points to a session that no longer exists as online, and only the offline session remains. The stated purpose of the PR is to let endpoints look up only the correct session type. For these tokens the encoded session type would point at the wrong (non-existent) session type. The offline_access case should be considered when computing the session type, or the limitation should at least be documented.

Grant shortcuts are not validated (null or length != 2)

`postInit` inserts `gtf.getShortcut()` into a `ConcurrentHashMap` without validating it. A third-party `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` returning null causes an NPE during server startup. A shortcut that is not exactly 2 chars makes tokens encode fine, but `getTokenContextFromTokenId` then throws `IllegalArgumentException` because it requires the context part to be exactly 6 chars. The existing duplicate check only covers collisions, and the lazy refresh paths in `getShortcutByGrantType`/`getGrantTypeByShortcut` skip validation too. Add an explicit startup check that every shortcut is non-null and exactly 2 characters, with a clear error message.

New abstract method breaks existing OAuth2GrantTypeFactory implementations

`getShortcut()` is added as an abstract method to a provider SPI interface. Any custom grant type factory compiled against the previous version fails to compile and, if already built, throws `AbstractMethodError` when `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit` calls it. Since the encoder already has an 'na' fallback, a default implementation would keep existing extensions working. If it is intentionally mandatory, this breaking change should be called out in the upgrade notes.

Access token `jti` format change is user-visible but undocumented

Access token IDs (`jti`, also logged in the `token_id` event detail) change from a plain UUID to `<6-char context>:<uuid>`. Clients, log pipelines, or custom extensions that assume the `jti` is a UUID will behave differently. This PR adds no release/upgrade note or documentation for the new format or the new `tokenContextEncoder` SPI, so operators have no notice of the change.

true_positives.golden_comment: After creating the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel, consider setting its id from the stored credential (e.g., myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()); otherwise getId() will be null and downstream removal by id (e.g., removeStoredCredentialById in the authenticator flow) may not work.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
User-storage recovery codes are never consumed, so they can be replayed and the same code is always requested

`isValid` for recovery codes only checks that the submitted code is in the stored JSON list and never marks it used. `getCredentials` (line ~237) rebuilds a fresh `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues(...)` from the full list on every call, so every code always looks unused. `RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean` therefore always asks for the same code number (index 0). Any code stays valid indefinitely, which breaks the one-time semantics of the local provider. The `allCodesUsed()` cleanup in `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator` can never trigger for federated credentials. The new model also has no id, because `createFromValues` does not carry over `recoveryCodes.getId()`, so `removeStoredCredentialById(model.getId())` would be called with a null id if it were ever reached. The new `getCredential()` path is exercised against a provider whose behavior diverges from the local provider on a core security property, and the test cannot detect that.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies the same bug: createFromValues does not carry over recoveryCodes.getId(), leaving the model id null and causing removeStoredCredentialById to be called with null. The additional replay discussion does not change the match.

false_positives.candidate:
getCredentials dereferences a possibly-null MyUser

`getMyUser(user)` returns null when the username is not in the `users` map, for example after `removeUser` or for a user from another provider instance. `getCredentials` then calls `myUser.recoveryCodes` immediately and throws an NPE. Every other method in this class (`isConfiguredFor`, `isValid`, `getDisableableCredentialTypesStream`) guards against null. Since `getFederatedCredentialsStream()` is now called from the login path via `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential`, this can turn a missing user into a 500.

Recovery codes can be created and validated in user storage but not disabled or removed

`supportsCredentialType`, `updateCredential`, `isConfiguredFor` and `isValid` now handle recovery codes. `getDisableableCredentialTypesStream` and `disableCredentialType` still only handle OTP. An admin therefore cannot see recovery codes as a disableable credential, and `disableCredentialType` logs "Unsupported to disable credential" and does nothing. Once recovery codes are written to the user storage they can never be removed through the admin API, which is inconsistent with the OTP handling next to it.

Creating codes in user storage leaves stale local recovery codes valid (and vice versa)

When `updateCredential` succeeds, the method returns without touching any existing recovery-codes credential in the local DB. The local `createCredential` path likewise ignores federated codes. If a user already has local recovery codes and the storage later accepts the type, regenerating codes in the storage does not invalidate the old local ones. `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential` prefers the federated credential while `isValid` can still accept the old local codes. The user then holds two live recovery-code sets, and regenerating codes does not revoke the previous set.

Undocumented SPI contract: plaintext JSON list of codes handed to user storage

`createRecoveryCodesCredential` serializes the raw (unhashed) recovery codes to a JSON array and passes them as the value of a `UserCredentialModel`. The local provider stores only hashes. The javadoc says nothing about this format, that the storage receives plaintext codes, or how the storage should report used/unused codes through `getCredentials` (see the replay problem above). Third-party `CredentialInputUpdater` implementations have to guess the contract, and storing plaintext codes is a security-relevant decision that should be stated. The provider id is also hard-coded as `"keycloak-recovery-authn-codes"` instead of using the factory constant.

Recovery-key test covers only one happy-path login

`testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin` sets up codes and logs in once with code index 0. It does not test a wrong code being rejected, a second login that should ask for the next code index, reuse of an already-used code, or the exhausted-codes path (`allCodesUsed` removal and re-adding the required action). The first two would have exposed that user-storage codes are never consumed. The flow also includes a pointless `delayed-authenticator` with a constant `delay` of 0 and a misspelled alias (`delayed-suthenticator-config`), which looks copy-pasted from another test.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Unsafe raw List deserialization without type safety. Calling Optional.get() directly on the Optional returned by RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) without checking isPresent() can lead to a NoSuchElementException if the Optional is empty.

false_positives.candidate:
Default-strategy test path never enables rolling-updates in the CR; the custom image build hides it

createInitialDeployment returns early when updateStrategy == null, before FeatureSpec.setEnabledFeatures(rolling-updates) is applied. The `null` case of testImageChange and testCacheMaxCount therefore runs without the feature in the CR. It only works because Dockerfile-custom-image now builds the image with `--features=rolling-updates`. The new operator docs say the feature must be enabled, "Otherwise, the Operator will fail", and that is how the default-strategy case is documented. The test neither verifies this nor matches it, and the image-level flag makes the CR-level setting redundant. A regression in how the feature gets enabled would not be caught. Apply the feature setting to both branches, or add a test that the update fails or reports a clear status when the feature is off.

Feature-disabled behaviour only checked for `metadata`, and the new exit code 4 is never asserted

The new FEATURE_DISABLED exit code (4) is a scripting contract documented in update-compatibility.adoc. testFeatureNotEnabled only checks the error text for the `metadata` subcommand and does not assert the exit code. The `check` subcommand has the same guard and no disabled-feature test. A regression that exits with 0 or 1, or drops the early return in `check`, would pass. Add assertions that the exit code is 4 for both subcommands. Also cover the renumbered RECREATE exit code (now 3) in testWrongVersions.

Macro hard-codes `--features=rolling-updates`, conflicting with the "use all your start options" instruction

The updatecompatibility macro appends a fixed `--features=rolling-updates` to every rendered example. The guide tells users to pass all the options they use with `start`, including `--features=...` in most real deployments. Following both instructions yields two `--features` options. Picocli rejects that or silently overrides one. Either way the metadata is computed against a different feature set than the running server, which is the case the warning in the guide describes. The guide should say that `rolling-updates` must be added to the existing feature list, rather than showing it as an extra standalone flag.

Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Event listener is now gated on V1 feature, so V2 gets no cleanup when a client is removed

The whole listener body is now wrapped in `Profile.isFeatureEnabled(ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ)`. This avoids calling the V2 `setPermissionsEnabled`, which throws UnsupportedOperationException. As a side effect, under V2 nothing reacts to `ClientRemovedEvent`. The per-client resource (named after the client UUID) and any scope permissions that reference it remain in the admin-permissions authorization store after the client is deleted. Stale resources and permissions accumulate and show up when permissions are listed. The change also silently drops the previous behaviour in realms where neither feature is enabled. A V2-specific cleanup handler is needed rather than just disabling the listener.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: the cleanup listener is incorrectly guarded by the V1 feature flag, so under V2-only the removal handler does not run and stale/orphaned permissions remain. The candidate focuses on client removal, which is within the golden comment's scope.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getClientsWithPermission uses findByType and returns resource names that are not necessarily client ids

`getClientsWithPermission` iterates `resourceStore.findByType(server, "Clients", ...)` and adds `resource.getName()` to the result. In `AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource`, per-client resources are created without a type, so they are not returned by `findByType`. The only resource with type `Clients` is the all-clients resource, whose name is the literal string "Clients", not a client id. If an all-clients permission grants the scope, the result is {"Clients"}, which matches no client. Clients granted individually are never returned. Callers that use this set to filter clients will get wrong results. Either the lookup must also cover per-client resources (and resolve names to client ids), or the method needs an all-clients expansion.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug in getClientsWithPermission: findByType only returns the type-level Clients resource, while per-client resources are untyped, so resource.getName() yields the literal "Clients" rather than actual client IDs and callers get incorrect results.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Possible NPE: getResourceTypeResource can return null and is passed to findByResource

`AdminPermissionsSchema.getResourceTypeResource(...)` returns null when the schema is not supported for the server (for example admin permissions disabled on the realm while the client still exists) or when the type resource is not found. The result is passed straight into `findByResource(server, resource)` and later dereferenced via `resource.getScopes()`, with no null check. That would turn a permission check into a 500 instead of a plain "false".
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same NPE risk: getResourceTypeResource may return null, and that result is passed into findByResource without a defensive null check.

true_positives.golden_comment: Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dead code and unused imports left in ClientPermissionsV2

The private `getEvaluationContext(...)` is never called. The `logger` field and the imports `Scope` and `TOKEN_EXCHANGE` are also unused. This looks like leftover scaffolding copied from the V1 class (including the token-exchange `kc.client.id` attribute), and it is misleading because V2 throws UnsupportedOperationException for token exchange. It should be removed.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies the same unused private getEvaluationContext method in ClientPermissionsV2 and recommends removal. Additional mentions of unused imports/logger do not change the core matching issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Javadoc for requireView() and requireViewClientScopes() says "Returns true" but they are void and throw

`requireView()` (lines 95-98) and `requireViewClientScopes()` (lines 100-103) are documented as "Returns {@code true} if canView()/canViewClientScopes() returns true". Both methods are `void` and throw ForbiddenException when the check fails. Every other `require*` method in this same interface is documented correctly as "Throws ForbiddenException if ...". These two should be fixed to match.

getResourceName does not handle the Clients resource type

`getResourceName` special-cases only `USERS` ("All users" for the type resource, the username for a per-user resource). For a policy whose resourceType is `Clients`, it falls through to `resource.getDisplayName()`. Per-client resources are created in `getOrCreateResource` via `resourceStore.create(server, name, owner)` with no display name, and their name is the client's internal UUID. So the "all clients" resource and each per-client resource resolve to a null or opaque name when permissions are rendered. Clients need the same handling: "All clients" for the type resource and the clientId for a specific client.

Up to five full policy evaluations per client in canView(client) when listing

`canView(client)` calls `canView()` (one evaluation on the all-clients resource), then `canConfigure(client)`. That calls `canManage(client)` (a second evaluation) and a CONFIGURE `hasPermission` (a third). Finally it calls `hasPermission(client, VIEW)` (a fourth). Each `hasPermission` does a resource lookup, possibly a policy-store lookup, and a full `evaluatePermission` over all of the resource's scopes. Only one scope is inspected afterwards. When listing clients this runs per client, so cost grows quickly with realm size. Evaluating once and checking several scopes, or passing only the requested scope to the evaluation, would avoid the repetition.

canView() ignores an all-clients MANAGE grant while canView(ClientScopeModel) honours it

`canView()` is `canViewClientDefault() || hasPermission(VIEW)`. An admin with only the all-clients MANAGE scope therefore fails `canView()`/`requireView()`. `canView(ClientScopeModel)` explicitly accepts `VIEW || MANAGE`, and `canView(ClientModel)` accepts manage indirectly through `canConfigure`. For users, the tests treat manage as implying view. Endpoints guarded by the no-arg `canView()`/`requireView()` will behave differently from per-client and client-scope checks for the same admin.

Test regenerates the secret of the client used to authenticate the admin client and mutates shared state without restoring it

`realmAdminClient` authenticates with client `myclient` and secret `mysecret`. `testConfigureOnlyOneClient` calls `clientResource.generateNewSecret()` on that same client. Once the secret is rotated, any later token acquisition or refresh by this admin client in the class (the token expires, or another test builds a new session) fails with 401 using the old secret. This makes the suite order- and timing-dependent. Other tests also leave persistent changes: they rename `myclient` and `realmClient`, move a default client scope to optional, and create roles on `myclient`. `onAfter` only removes permissions, so these mutations leak into subsequent tests.

No coverage for several new V2 client paths

The new tests cover manage, configure, view and map-roles(+composite) on clients. There is no test for `MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE`. Nothing checks that a client with a CONFIGURE or VIEW permission still cannot be managed or modified beyond what is intended. `getClientsWithPermission` and the client-scope management permissions (`canManageClientScopes`, `canView(ClientScopeModel)`) are not exercised either. The `getClientsWithPermission` path is the one with the likely defects noted above, and a test would have exposed them.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.

true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
V2 canManage() grants global group management for the VIEW scope

`canManage()` falls back to `hasPermission(null, VIEW, MANAGE)`, so a view-only permission on the "all groups" resource is enough to pass it. This is the check behind `GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup` (`auth.groups().requireManage()`). An admin who was granted only `view` on all groups can therefore create top-level groups. The per-group `canManage(GroupModel)` correctly uses only `MANAGE`, and the V1 equivalent requires the manage-users role, so this looks like a copy-paste from `canView()`. The Javadoc in `GroupPermissionEvaluator` repeats the same wrong contract. No test covers a VIEW-only admin attempting a manage operation. Change the call to `hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that canManage() incorrectly accepts VIEW scope via the fallback permission check, allowing view-only users to perform management operations; the fix is to check only MANAGE.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission uses resource IDs where group IDs (resource names) are needed

In V2 the authorization resource for a group is named after the group ID (see `AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup`, and `hasPermission` looks it up with `resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId)`). The callback here passes `groupResource.getId()`, which is the resource's own UUID, to `hasPermission`. That lookup by name never matches, so evaluation silently falls back to the generic "Groups" type resource and ignores the per-group permission. The method then adds `groupResource.getId()` to the result set, but callers (`UsersResource.searchForUser`, `getUsersCount`, `BruteForceUsersResource`) treat the values as group IDs for `UserModel.GROUPS` and `getUsersCount(..., groupIds)`. The result is wrong or empty sets and wrong user counts. For searches, the group restriction is not applied in the query, so the later per-user `canView` filter runs after `first`/`max` pagination and returns short or empty pages. The new test only checks the unpaginated search, where the post-filter hides the problem. Use `groupResource.getName()` for both the evaluation and the result, and skip the type-level resource whose name is "Groups".
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug in getGroupIdsWithViewPermission: it uses the authorization resource UUID (getId()) for hasPermission and the returned set, but hasPermission resolves by resource name and callers expect underlying group IDs, causing fallback to the type-level Groups resource and incorrect filtering/counts. The candidate's extra details are consistent with the golden issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Possible NPE when the Groups type resource does not exist

`getResourceTypeResource` returns null when the "Groups" resource has not been created. false_positives.candidate:
Error timestamps (seconds) compared against replay event timestamps (milliseconds)

`gen_request_data` interleaves errors with breadcrumbs by checking `error_events[idx]["timestamp"] < event.get("timestamp", 0)`. The error timestamp comes from the nodestore event payload, which is epoch seconds. The `event["timestamp"]` from an rrweb replay segment is normally epoch milliseconds. With real data every error then compares as 'earlier' than the first replay event, so all errors are emitted at the start of the log instead of in chronological order. The Seer summary receives a wrong timeline. The tests use the same unit for both sides (`now.timestamp()` for both, and small numbers in `test_get_request_data`), so they cannot catch this. `get_environment_info` calls `issue.get_recommended_event()` for every issue in the comment (up to 5). That performs an event lookup (Snuba plus nodestore) per issue, synchronously in the comment-building path, just to show an environment name. `MERGED_PR_SINGLE_ISSUE_TEMPLATE` puts the raw (user-controlled) issue title inside `[**{title}**]({url})`. One report of an unlisted type discards all valid reports in the same request. The previous code only used the types as hints and accepted everything. For a data-collection endpoint it is safer to skip or tag unknown types than to fail the batch.

The old `cacheMu.Lock()` held for the whole of `BuildIndex` did more than serialize writes. `GetIndex` takes `RLock`, so it blocked while any build was running, and a second caller then found the freshly cached index. After this change `GetIndex` returns nil while a build is in progress. `searchSupport.getOrCreateIndex` (Search requests and the watch-event handler) can therefore start a second `BuildIndex` for the same key, and the search code has only a TODO about this. For file-backed indexes the second `bleve.New(dir, ...)` hits an existing path and fails, so the search errors or the watch event is dropped. For memory indexes the work is duplicated, the `IndexTenants` and `IndexedKinds` metrics are double-counted, and the first index is overwritten in the cache without being closed. A per-key singleflight or in-progress map is needed once the global lock is gone.

This PR adds a `TotalDocs()` call at the end of `searchSupport.init`, after the watch goroutine has already started. A watch event that triggers a lazy build of another index can therefore write the map while it is being iterated. With `WorkerThreads > 1`, which is the case this PR optimizes, this is a data race. A worker can also `return err` after another worker has overwritten the shared variable. A failed build can then be reported as nil, so startup init silently succeeds with a missing index, or it reports another goroutine's error. Now that init runs at startup this path always executes. Use a local `err` inside the closure and `atomic.Int64` for the counter.

The test is skipped for postgres with 'not working with postgres in Drone'. It exercises the storage-server target, which now runs `ResourceServer.Init` synchronously at construction: backend DB init, index build and watcher start. A test that starts failing in CI right after eager init was introduced is a strong sign of a startup ordering or DB-readiness problem, such as tables or migrations not being ready when the server is built. Skipping it hides that signal, and the 'works locally' claim is unverified. `Stop` sets `s.initErr` to 'service is stopping' or 'service is stopped'. This worked because every handler called `s.Init(ctx)`, which returns `s.initErr` after the `sync.Once`. With those calls removed, nothing reads `initErr` any more. After `Stop`, Create, Update, Delete, Read, List, Watch, Search and the blob endpoints keep running against a stopped backend and a cancelled server context. `IsHealthy` also no longer reports an unhealthy state when the server is stopping. Either keep a cheap stopped check in the handlers or drop the dead `initErr` writes in `Stop`.

When `s.Init(ctx)` fails, `NewResourceServer` returns `nil, err` without calling `cancel()` or `lifecycle.Stop`. Previously the server object stayed reachable and could be stopped. Call `cancel()` and best-effort `lifecycle.Stop` on the error path. The PR is described as fixing trace propagation, but only `GetResourceStats` was changed to keep the span context. `WriteEvent` here still does `_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, ...)`. The child spans (create/update/delete, the list queries, the bleve index writes) are parented to the caller's span instead of the new one, so traces are still flattened or mis-parented. Use `ctx, span :=` in these places as well.

false_positives.candidate:
Strategy close()/terminate() shuts down the factory-owned queue pool, so messages are silently dropped and committed after the first rebalance

The `FixedQueuePool` and its `OffsetTracker` are created once in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` and shared by every strategy from `create_with_partitions`. Arroyo calls `close()`/`join()` on the strategy at every rebalance, and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()`/`terminate()` call `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`. That permanently shuts down all queues and workers. The factory still holds the dead pool (`queue_pool` is only set to None in `factory.shutdown()`), so the next strategy gets the same pool. Every `work_queue.put()` then raises `queue.ShutDown`. `submit()` catches `Exception`, marks the offset as added and completed, and moves on. The result is that after the first rebalance every message is dropped without being processed, and its offset is still committed. The tracker also keeps `last_committed`, `all_offsets` and `outstanding` for partitions that were revoked or reassigned. The strategy should not own the shared pool's lifecycle. Either build the pool and tracker per strategy, or leave them running in `close()` and only stop them from `factory.shutdown()`.

Offsets are committed from a background thread, but arroyo's commit callback and KafkaConsumer are not thread-safe

`_commit_loop` runs on its own daemon thread and calls `self.commit_function(...)`, which wraps arroyo's `commit` callback. That callback stages and commits offsets on the `KafkaConsumer`, whose state is owned by the main `StreamProcessor` thread; arroyo does not support calling it concurrently with `poll`/`_run_once`. This can race with the main thread's own consumer calls. It can also commit offsets for partitions that have just been revoked, which makes `stage_offsets` raise. When that raise happens, `mark_committed` is skipped. The tracker never forgets the revoked partition, so the same failing commit is retried and logged every second indefinitely. Commits should be handed back to the main thread, for example by recording the committable offsets and calling `commit` from `poll()`.

Queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure despite the class docstring promising it

`queue.Queue()` is created without `maxsize`, and `submit()` never blocks or raises `MessageRejected`. The strategy's docstring claims "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but there is none. If any worker is slow (the exact scenario this PR targets) or the DB is degraded, the consumer keeps reading from Kafka at full speed. Queue depth, the `WorkItem`s (which hold the full Kafka message) and the offset tracker sets all grow without bound, which risks OOM. Meanwhile no offsets are committed because commits are contiguous. Use a bounded queue and translate a full queue into `MessageRejected` so arroyo applies backpressure, or at least fix the docstring.

Commit logic assumes strictly contiguous Kafka offsets and stalls permanently on any gap

`get_committable_offsets` walks `range(start, max_offset + 1)` and stops at the first offset that is not in `all_offsets`. Kafka partitions can legitimately have non-consecutive offsets (compaction, transaction control records, messages skipped or filtered upstream). After `mark_committed` trims the set, a single missing offset means `highest_committable` never advances past it. The consumer then stops committing for that partition forever, `all_offsets` grows without bound, and a restart replays everything since the gap. `test_offset_gaps_block_commits` encodes this behavior as desired. A safer approach is to track only the offsets actually submitted, in order, and commit up to the smallest outstanding offset.

Shutdown joins workers sequentially with 5s each, never flushes a final commit, and 'graceful' drain is not honored

`FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` joins each worker with a 5s timeout one after another. If several workers are busy, `terminate()` or `close()` can block for up to 5s × num_queues (100s with the default 20), which stalls rebalances and shutdown. `worker.shutdown = True` also makes workers exit after the current item, so `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` never actually drains the remaining queued items. Neither `close()` nor `terminate()` does a final commit of offsets that finished processing since the last 1s tick, so those messages are reprocessed on restart. `join(timeout)` also ignores its timeout argument.

Distribution test is flaky because str hash is randomized per process, and the ordering/concurrency tests do not check ordering or concurrency

`test_different_groups_distributed` asserts that 20 string group keys cover all 3 queues. `hash(str)` is salted per interpreter run, so there is roughly a 0.1% chance on any run that some queue is never hit, which makes the test flaky. Separately, `test_preserves_order_within_group` and `test_concurrent_processing_different_groups` in the strategy tests only check that the result count equals the number submitted, even though their names and docstrings claim ordering and concurrency are verified. `test_concurrent_processing_across_groups` has the same problem, since it never checks that groups actually run in parallel.

false_positives.candidate:
upsampled_count uses sum(sample_weight) with no NULL handling

The new aggregate is `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))`. Events stored before `sample_weight` was populated, or without a client sample rate, have NULL in that column. `sum` skips NULLs, so those events are counted as 0, or the whole bucket becomes NULL and `toInt64` then yields 0 or an error. Allowlisted projects therefore show undercounted or zeroed error charts as soon as their data contains any unweighted events. The comment says the schema guarantees the column exists, but a nullable column existing does not mean it is populated. It should be `sum(ifNull(sample_weight, 1))` so unweighted events count as 1. Also, the function is registered as a public (non-private) discover function. Users can call `upsampled_count()` directly, including on datasets or event types where `sample_weight` does not exist.

`_is_error_focused_query` returns True if the raw lowercase query string contains `event.type:error`. That matches `!event.type:error` (the opposite intent), `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction`, and any query where the text appears inside a longer token or value. In those cases `count()` is rewritten to `sum(sample_weight)` over transaction or other non-error rows, which have no sample weight. The result is wrong counts or Snuba errors. The docstring claims this errs on the side of caution, but a substring match does the opposite. It needs to parse the query, or at least check token boundaries and negation.

The NOTE on `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` says it reads the allowlist fresh each time so the latest configuration is always used. The caller wraps it in a 60-second cache, so results can be up to a minute stale. Comments in the endpoint make similar claims ("cached result ensures consistent behavior", "most current schema assumptions", "better query optimization and caching") that are not true of the code. They will mislead maintainers about when the allowlist takes effect.

Upsampling transform applied in RPC branches that can never be eligible

`use_rpc` is only true for `spans_rpc` and `ourlogs`. `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` returns False for every dataset other than errors and discover, so `upsampling_enabled` is always False in the two RPC branches (top-events and timeseries). The `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` calls there are dead code. They also suggest to readers that RPC datasets are supported, and they would feed a non-RPC `upsampled_count() as count` column into the RPC `y_axes` if the gating ever changed.

Endpoint tests miss top_events, negated queries, the cache path and the dashboard split path

The new tests only cover plain timeseries with `count()`. They do not cover the `topEvents` branch where the transform is also applied. They do not cover `!event.type:error` or compound queries, which the substring check mishandles. They do not cover events with NULL `sample_weight`, the likely failure for `sum(sample_weight)`. They do not cover the dashboard split path, where the outer `dataset` is used instead of the scoped one. The tests also mock `options` while using the real cache, and `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` and `invalidate_upsampling_cache` have no direct unit tests. The 60s cache and the unused invalidation are therefore untested.

A new `sentry-repo` entry is added as a git submodule pointer (`Subproject commit a5d2909...`, the base commit). It is unrelated to the feature and has no corresponding `.gitmodules` entry, so it looks like an accidental commit of a local checkout. It can break `git submodule` operations and should be removed from the PR.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Every distinct denied resource now triggers a full DB permission re-query

In `Check`, when the cached scope map does not allow the request, the code always falls through to `getIdentityPermissions`. That runs `GetUserBasicRole`, `ListUserTeams` and `GetUserPermissions` against the DB, and `getUserPermissions` no longer short-circuits on the cache. The denial cache is keyed per (user, action, name, parent), so it only helps for repeats of the exact same resource. A user who is legitimately denied on many different dashboards or folders, for example a UI list of items or a scan, causes one DB permission query per distinct resource within each 30s window. Singleflight only merges concurrent calls. This removes most of the protection the permission cache gave and can amplify load on the DB. Consider rate-limiting the refresh per user/action, or negative-caching at the (user, action) level for a short time after a refresh.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same Check cache behavior: cached denials are not trusted and fall through to a fresh database permission lookup. The candidate emphasizes the resulting DB load, while the golden comment emphasizes the security implication, but the underlying issue is the same.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial-cache test passes even if the denial cache is ignored

The test comment says it allows access in `permCache` 'to prove this is not checked', but the cached map is `{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}`, which also denies. Without the denial-cache lookup, `Check` would see a cached deny, fall back to the default `fakeStore` (no permissions), and still return `Allowed=false`. The test therefore cannot tell whether the denial short-circuit works. It should seed an allowing permission (`true`, or a store that grants access) and assert the store is not called. There is also no test that a DB-confirmed deny populates `permDenialCache`, and none that a later identical check skips the DB.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify that the test's cached permission map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so it denies rather than allowing access and cannot prove the denial-cache behavior.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key is ambiguous because fields are joined with '_' and names can contain '_'

The key is `ns.perm_<uid>_<action>_<name>_<parent>`, and Grafana dashboard and folder UIDs may contain underscores. `name="a_b", parent="c"` and `name="a", parent="b_c"` produce the same key, so a denial for one resource denies the other for the whole TTL. The key also shares the `.perm_<uid>_<action>` prefix with `userPermCacheKey`, so the two caches are only kept apart by their value types. Use a distinct prefix such as `perm_denial_` and a separator that cannot occur in the fields, or hash the parts.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe ambiguous denial cache keys from joining fields with underscores, allowing collisions when names/parents contain underscores and causing incorrect permission denials.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache key omits identity type, so denials leak between anonymous and render subjects

`userPermDenialCacheKey` is built from namespace, `checkReq.UserUID`, action, name and parent. The identity type is not part of the key. `Check` reads the denial cache before it looks at `IdentityType`. `anonymous:0` and `render:0` both have UID `0`, so they share a key. The existing permission cache avoids this by using a separate `anonymousPermCacheKey`. If anonymous is denied `dashboards:read` on dash1, a later `render:0` check for the same dashboard hits that entry and is wrongly denied, even though the renderer is granted read on everything. The reverse also happens: a render denial for a write action can deny an anonymous Editor. Include the identity type in the key, or use a separate prefix per type.

Denials computed from a possibly stale folder tree are cached with no invalidation

After the DB re-query, `checkPermission` calls `checkInheritedPermissions`, which uses `buildFolderTree`. That tree is itself cached for 30s and is not refreshed by the permission re-query. For a newly created nested folder whose permission comes only from an ancestor, the stale tree does not contain the folder, so the check is denied. That result is then stored in the denial cache for another 30s, with no way to clear it when the folder tree or the user's permissions change. Access to newly created resources can stay denied for up to a minute even though the re-query was meant to fix exactly this case.

true_positives.golden_comment: OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OAuth `state` is a static, guessable value, so it gives no CSRF protection

`state` is `pipeline.signature`, which the tests pin to the constant `9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3`. That is a deterministic hash of the pipeline view classes, not a per-flow random nonce. Every user and session therefore gets the same value, and an attacker can craft `/extensions/github/setup/?code=...&state=<known>` links that pass the check. An OAuth `state` must be unpredictable and tied to the user's session. Also, `!=` is a non-constant-time comparison; use `constant_time_compare`. As written, the PR's claim that a mismatching `state` is rejected adds little real protection.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same core bug: OAuth state is set to pipeline.signature, a static deterministic value, instead of a per-request random nonce, so it provides no CSRF protection.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation

`integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` assumes every pre-existing Integration carries webhook-provided `sender` metadata. `build_integration` only sets `sender` from `state.get("sender")`, and nothing in this pipeline ever binds that key. The updated `test_basic_flow` also shows an Integration created through the pipeline with no `sender` in its metadata. If such an Integration remains without an OrganizationIntegration, for example after one org is uninstalled, a legacy record, or an install created through the pipeline, this lookup raises `KeyError`. The user gets a 500 instead of the friendly error page, and the install is blocked. Use `.get("sender", {}).get("login")` and treat a missing sender as a controlled failure, or define explicit behaviour for it.

The candidate adds context and a suggested fix, but the underlying issue is identical.

false_positives.candidate:
Authenticated-user check is skipped whenever the Integration row doesn't exist yet

The new `github_authenticated_user` vs `sender.login` comparison only runs when an Integration with that `external_id` already exists. It is created by the `installation` webhook. When `Integration.DoesNotExist` is raised, the code calls `pipeline.next_step()` without checking that the OAuth-authenticated user is the one who installed the app. Anyone who learns an installation_id can therefore finish the pipeline before the webhook has been processed, or if it was delayed or lost, and bind someone else's installation to their org. The check depends on a webhook race. A robust fix would verify against GitHub directly, for example by confirming the installation appears in `GET /user/installations` for the user token. The OAuth user token is already available at that point but is discarded after reading `login`.

Network and HTTP errors in the token exchange and user lookup are not handled

Only `safe_urlread` and decoding are inside the `try`. `safe_urlopen(...)` on line 423 can raise connection, timeout or SSL errors, and `get_user_info(...)` on line 434 calls `raise_for_status()`, so an invalid or expired token raises `HTTPError`. Either failure surfaces as an unhandled 500 in the middle of the install dialog, not the 'Invalid installation request' page the PR describes for these cases. The existing `OAuth2CallbackView.exchange_token`, which this code is modelled on, wraps the whole exchange in exception handling. The failure paths also log nothing, so a failed exchange gives support and debugging no signal.

The test now sends `state=ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05`, which differs from the pipeline signature `9cae5e...`. The request is therefore rejected by the `state` mismatch check in `OAuthLoginView` before the 404 from `/app/installations/...` is ever reached. It asserts the generic 'Invalid installation request.' text. So it now covers state mismatch under a misleading name, and the `The GitHub installation could not be found.` branch in `build_integration` has lost its coverage. Use the valid state for this test, and add a separate test for state mismatch.

New failure and success paths of the validation are untested

Only the user-mismatch case is covered, and only incidentally the state mismatch. There are no tests for: a failed token exchange (no `access_token` in the response); a `/user` response without `login`; or the positive case where an Integration with webhook-provided `sender` already exists, has no OrganizationIntegration, and the authenticated user matches. That last case is the main new success path of `GitHubInstallation`. There is also no test for an existing Integration lacking `sender` metadata, which would currently raise `KeyError`. `assert_setup_flow` additionally hard-codes `responses.calls[2]`, which silently breaks whenever the number of HTTP calls in the flow changes.

The override test only rejects a slot if `slotEnd <= override.start` or `slotStart > override.end`. A slot that starts before the override and ends inside it is accepted. A slot that starts inside the override and ends after `override.end` is accepted. A slot starting exactly at `override.end` is accepted, because `isAfter` is strict. This is the situation the PR is meant to prevent (RR events booked when the fixed host is unavailable). The condition should be that the whole slot lies in `[override.start, override.end]`, i.e. reject when `slotStart < start` or `slotEnd > end`.

Only afterwards is the invitee-organizer offset added and reduced to `hour()*60+minute()`. Two problems follow. (1) If the shift pushes the start/end past midnight, the minutes wrap modulo 24h, so start or end becomes a small number and the range is either dropped (`start >= end` is skipped in `buildSlots`) or shown on the wrong day. (2) The day the override is attached to is computed before the shift. With a large timezone gap (e.g. organizer in Kolkata with a 20:00-23:00 override, invitee in Tokyo) the override can be attached to the day after the one it really falls on. false_positives.candidate:
Attendees are persisted before the calendar update with no error handling or rollback

The DB update that creates the attendees runs first. `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees` follows with no try/catch. If the calendar update throws, the client sees an error but the guests are already stored and no emails are sent. A retry then filters those guests out as duplicates and fails with `emails_must_be_unique_valid`, so the user cannot complete the operation. The calendar and DB state are left inconsistent. Handle calendar failures explicitly, or reorder the steps and roll back.

Calendar update uses the caller's credentials rather than the organizer's

`EventManager` is built from `getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` and `...user`. The route also permits attendees and team admins to add guests. For those callers the credentials do not belong to the user whose calendar holds the event, so `updateCalendarAttendees` will fail or silently skip the external event. The organizer's calendar (`booking.user`, which is already loaded with its credentials) is the one that should be updated.

Any attendee can add an unbounded number of arbitrary guests, which sends emails to arbitrary addresses

Any logged-in user whose email matches an attendee of the booking is authorized. Neither `ZAddGuestsInputSchema` nor the handler limits the array size, and the booking status is not checked. A single call with many addresses triggers organizer, team and per-attendee emails and ICS invites to third parties, which makes it a spam vector. The attendee check is also case-sensitive on `user.email`. Add a max count, tighten who may add guests, and consider rejecting cancelled/rejected bookings.

CalendarEvent has no `team`, so the team-member email loop in sendAddGuestsEmails never runs

`evt` is built without `team` or any team member info, but `sendAddGuestsEmails` iterates `calendarEvent.team?.members` to notify the other hosts. For collective and round-robin team events that loop is dead code, and the other hosts are never told about the new guests. The subject also falls back to the organizer's name instead of the team name. Other fields such as `responses` and `bookerUrl` are missing too, which can degrade the email content.

Case-sensitive match on new guest email

`newGuests.includes(attendee.email)` compares strings exactly. The attendee emails come from the DB and the guest list from user input, so a casing difference sends a new guest the 'guests added' notification instead of the full scheduled invite.

isInvalidEmail is never cleared on success or on dialog dismiss

`isInvalidEmail` is set when validation fails and is only reset by the Cancel button. If the user triggers the error, corrects the emails and submits successfully, `onSuccess` resets the values but not the flag. The error banner then reappears the next time the dialog opens. Closing the dialog via overlay or Esc (`onOpenChange`) also keeps stale emails and error state.

Error toast is always prefixed with the code and the fallback message is unreachable

`message` is built as `${err.data?.code}: ${t(err.message)}`, which is always a non-empty string. `|| t("unable_to_add_guests")` can therefore never run, and users see raw text like `BAD_REQUEST: Emails must be unique and valid` or `undefined: ...`. The new `unable_to_add_guests` string is dead. Also, `handleAdd` silently returns when the email list is empty.

Hardcoded English tooltip and a label not bound to an input

The tooltip `"Remove email"` is not passed through `t()`, unlike the rest of the component. The `<label htmlFor="emails">` references an id that no input has, so the label is not associated with the fields. Rows use `key={index}`, which is fragile when entries are removed from the middle of the list.

Email failures are swallowed without logging the error

The catch block only logs a fixed string with `console.log` and drops `err`. If sending fails, the user still gets a 'Guests added' success and operators have nothing to diagnose it. At minimum log the error through the project logger.

Blacklisted or duplicate guests are silently dropped and the all-filtered error is misleading

If only some of the submitted guests are filtered out (existing attendee or blacklisted), the request still succeeds and the UI shows 'Guests added', with no indication that some were skipped. If all are filtered, the user gets 'Emails must be unique and valid' even when the cause is the blacklist. The response should report what was actually added or skipped.

New feature ships without any tests

The PR adds a mutation with non-trivial authorization, filtering and email logic, plus new UI and email templates, but no handler unit tests or e2e tests. true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup code consumption is a non-atomic read-modify-write

The code reads the encrypted blob, finds the index, nulls the entry, re-encrypts and writes the whole blob back, with no lock or compare-and-swap. Two concurrent logins using the same single-use code can both pass the `indexOf` check before either write lands. Both then succeed, violating the "can be used exactly once" guarantee. Concurrent logins using different codes can also overwrite each other's update and resurrect a used code. Use a transaction or optimistic concurrency, for example update where `backupCodes` equals the value that was read.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same non-atomic read-modify-write race in backup code consumption, where concurrent requests can reuse a single-use code.

Backup-code login can skip password verification by also sending a dummy totpCode

The password is only verified when `!credentials.totpCode` (line 121, unchanged). The new branch at line 131 is chosen when `credentials.backupCode` is present, and it never looks at `totpCode`. An attacker can send `email` + any non-empty `totpCode` + a valid `backupCode`. The password check is skipped and the backup-code branch authenticates the request. A single secret (a 40-bit backup code) then replaces both password and second factor. The PR adds a new credential path on top of this guard without tightening it. The Cancel button is hidden there. If the user dismisses the dialog via Escape, the overlay or the X (`onOpenChange`), the parent is never told 2FA was enabled, so the settings UI can still show it as off. The wizard also stays on `DisplayBackupCodes`, so reopening it shows stale codes. The user may never have saved the codes either. The dismiss path should be handled the same way as Close, or dismissal should be blocked on this step.

"missing_backup_codes" message points to a settings feature that does not exist

Users who enabled 2FA before this migration have `backupCodes = null`. When they click "Lost access" they get "No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings." There is no UI or endpoint to generate or regenerate backup codes for an already-enabled account. The only way to get codes is to disable 2FA, which requires a TOTP code or backup code they no longer have. The message gives an impossible instruction. Either add a regenerate flow or change the message to something actionable.

Unvalidated backupCode type can crash the disable endpoint

`req.body.backupCode` is only checked for truthiness, then `.replaceAll` is called on it. A non-string truthy value (number, object, array) throws a TypeError and returns a 500 instead of a 400 `IncorrectBackupCode`. Validate that it is a string before use, and ideally trim it.

Empty backup code submit silently does nothing on the login form

The login form uses `noValidate`, so the `required`/`minLength` attributes on the BackupCode input are not enforced. Submitting an empty backup code sends `backupCode: ""`, which is falsy. The server falls through to the TOTP branch and returns `SecondFactorRequired`. The handler then just calls `setTwoFactorRequired(true)` (already true), with no error shown. The user sees nothing happen. Handle the empty case client-side or show an error.

No test coverage for logging in or disabling 2FA with a backup code

The core new behaviour is untested, and the PR checklist admits no tests were added. The e2e changes only click download/copy/close on the new screen, and the file/clipboard contents are TODOs. Nothing exercises backup-code login, one-time consumption of a code, disabling 2FA with a backup code, or the MissingBackupCodes/IncorrectBackupCode paths. The first test ("enable and login") never closes the new backup-codes dialog. Its `isChecked()` assertion is always truthy, as the FIXME admits, so it does not verify the new step. Copy button shows success toast without awaiting the clipboard write

`navigator.clipboard.writeText(...)` returns a promise that is neither awaited nor caught, and the success toast is shown immediately. tabIndex={-1} on the shared password visibility toggle removes it from keyboard navigation

Destination calendars without credentialId no longer used when creating Google events

The target calendar is now chosen only by `cal.credentialId === credentialId`. For those legacy destinations nothing matches, so Google events are always created in `primary` instead of the configured `destination.externalId`. `createEvent` filters the account's calendars by the first (main host) destination calendar's externalId. For a second host's CalDAV credential, none of its calendars match the main host's externalId, so the filtered list is empty, `Promise.all([])` resolves, and `createEvent` returns success without creating anything. That host silently gets no calendar event. The method needs to use the destination calendar belonging to the credential being used (as Google does with `credentialId`).

Both services take `event.destinationCalendar[0].externalId` as the calendar id, regardless of which credential the call is made with. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. The function also continues to send emails and returns `true` before the calendar and video deletions finish. In serverless environments the work can be cut off. Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...))` inside the try block.

false_positives.candidate:
import() calls in the object literal run eagerly, so every app still loads at module evaluation

Each entry is `import("./x")` evaluated directly in the object literal. All ~29 dynamic imports start the moment `@calcom/app-store` is first imported, so every app package is still loaded on first use of the store. This gives no lazy loading, and the module graph still pulls in every app. It also adds overhead: the promises are created up front, and call sites must now `await` them. An app whose import fails produces an unhandled rejection at startup. It then rejects on every later lookup instead of being skipped. To get lazy behaviour, store thunks (`() => import("./x")`) and invoke only the one needed.

async forEach callback inside try/catch: errors are no longer caught and deletions are not awaited

Same issue as the vital reschedule. `forEach(async ...)` discards the promises, so the `try/catch` around it is now dead for any rejection from `getCalendar`, `deleteEvent` or `deleteMeeting`; these become unhandled rejections. The reschedule flow does not wait for the external deletions before sending emails and returning. Replace with `await Promise.all(refs.map(async ...))` so errors are logged and the work completes.

Making the `forEach` callback async to `await getCalendar` means the mutation neither awaits nor handles failures of `getCalendar`, `deleteEvent` or `deleteMeeting`. There is no `try/catch` here at all. A failing integration produces an unhandled rejection, which can crash the Node process or be silently dropped. The mutation also returns, after sending emails and webhooks, before the external events are actually removed. Collect the promises and `await Promise.all(...)`, with error handling.

Recurring-cancel path pushes into apiDeletes from an unawaited async forEach, after Promise.all has already run

In the `allRemainingBookings` branch, `.forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(credential); ... apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent) })` is not awaited. It also pushes the resolved result rather than the promise. `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` runs later and sees an `apiDeletes` array that these callbacks have not populated yet. The calendar deletions for recurring bookings are therefore never awaited, and their failures are unhandled rejections. Adding `await getCalendar` inside the callback delays the first `deleteEvent` call further, so a response (or serverless freeze) can happen before any deletion starts. Replace with a `for...of` loop or `Promise.all(map(...))` and push the promises.
